title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text: A “paradox” here doesn’t mean something impossible — it means something that is mathematically true but goes against what our intuition expects. These come up constantly in real data: in medicine, sports, hiring, machine learning, and everyday probability. Each section below explains one paradox in plain language, shows the R code that simulates or visualizes it, and displays the resulting graph on its own so it’s easy to study in isolation.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text: A “paradox” here doesn’t mean something impossible — it means something that is mathematically true but goes against what our intuition expects. These come up constantly in real data: in medicine, sports, hiring, machine learning, and everyday probability. Each section below explains one paradox in plain language, shows the R code that simulates or visualizes it, and displays the resulting graph on its own so it’s easy to study in isolation.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Simpson’s Paradox
The idea: A trend can be true in every single subgroup of your data, yet completely reverse once you combine all the groups together. Imagine three schools where students who study more score higher within each school — but the school where students study most has the lowest-scoring intake, so across all schools combined, more study looks linked to lower scores. Nothing dishonest is happening; it’s just a consequence of how the groups sit relative to each other.


Code
set.seed(42)
n <- 40

# Three groups: each has a positive local slope,
# but they're staggered so the global slope is negative.
make_group <- function(mx, my, label) {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean = mx, sd = 0.6)
  y <- my + 0.9 * (x - mx) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4)
  data.frame(x = x, y = y, group = label)
}

dat <- rbind(
  make_group(mx = 2, my = 8, label = "Group A"),
  make_group(mx = 5, my = 5, label = "Group B"),
  make_group(mx = 8, my = 2, label = "Group C")
)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  # Overall (aggregated) trend — negative
  geom_smooth(
    method  = "lm", se = FALSE,
    color   = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  # Per-group trends — positive
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = group),
    method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  # Points
  geom_point(aes(color = group), size = 2.8, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Group A" = "#E74C3C",
               "Group B" = "#27AE60",
               "Group C" = "#2980B9")
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 6.5, y = 8.6, label = "Overall trend\n(aggregated)",
    size = 3.5, color = "black", fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Simpson's Paradox",
    subtitle = "Within each group the slope is positive — yet the overall slope (dashed) is negative",
    x        = "X",
    y        = "Y",
    color    = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
  )









Each colored line (one per group) slopes upward. But the dashed black line — fit across all the points at once, ignoring group membership — slopes downward. Always check whether a relationship holds within subgroups before trusting an overall trend.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Infinitely Many Perfect Fits (Overfitting)
The idea: With only a handful of data points, there isn’t just one curve that fits them perfectly — there are infinitely many. Here we start with 4 points and a cubic curve that passes through all of them exactly (R² = 1, a “perfect” fit). Then we show that we can wiggle that curve in endless different ways, and every single variant still passes through all 4 points with the same perfect R². A perfect fit on tiny or noisy data doesn’t mean you’ve found the truth — it can just mean the model is flexible enough to memorize whatever points you gave it. This is the core intuition behind overfitting.


Code
# --- 4 data points ---
pts <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2, 4, 5),
  y = c(2, 5, 3, 7)
)

# --- Base: unique cubic interpolant through all 4 points ---
fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3, raw = TRUE), data = pts)

x_seq <- seq(0.3, 5.7, length.out = 600)
y_base <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = x_seq))

# --- "Wiggle" term: zero at every data point, so adding it keeps R²=1 ---
wiggle <- (x_seq - pts$x[1]) *
  (x_seq - pts$x[2]) *
  (x_seq - pts$x[3]) *
  (x_seq - pts$x[4])

# --- Build family of perfect-fit curves by varying c ---
c_vals  <- c(0, 0.25, -0.25, 0.55, -0.55)
c_labels <- c("c = 0  (cubic)", "c = 0.25", "c = -0.25", "c = 0.55", "c = -0.55")

curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(c_vals), function(i) {
  data.frame(
    x     = x_seq,
    y     = y_base + c_vals[i] * wiggle,
    curve = c_labels[i]
  )
}))

curves$curve <- factor(curves$curve, levels = c_labels)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data  = curves,
    aes(x = x, y = y, color = curve, linewidth = curve == "c = 0  (cubic)"),
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.4, `FALSE` = 0.9), guide = "none") +
  geom_point(
    data  = pts,
    aes(x = x, y = y),
    size  = 4, shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "black", stroke = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "c = 0  (cubic)" = "#E74C3C",
      "c = 0.25"       = "#3498DB",
      "c = -0.25"      = "#27AE60",
      "c = 0.55"       = "#9B59B6",
      "c = -0.55"      = "#F39C12"
    )
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 0.4, y = 20,
    label    = "All curves pass through\nevery point  (R² = 1)",
    hjust    = 0, size = 3.6, color = "grey30", fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Infinitely Many Perfect Fits",
    subtitle = expression(
      "Each curve = cubic interpolant + " * italic(c) * " · (x−x[1])(x−x[2])(x−x[3])(x−x[4])"
    ),
    x     = "x",
    y     = "y",
    color = "Curve"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 10),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









Notice how wildly the curves diverge away from the 4 known points, even though they agree perfectly at those points. Between and beyond the data, they tell completely different stories — a warning against trusting a model just because it fits your training data perfectly.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Anscombe’s Quartet
The idea: Four datasets can have nearly identical means, variances, correlations, and best-fit regression lines (equal to two or three decimal places) — while looking nothing alike when plotted. One is a clean straight-line relationship, one is a curve, one has a single outlier bending an otherwise perfect line, and one is a vertical cluster distorted by a single extreme point. The lesson: summary statistics can hide very different realities. Always plot your data.


Code
t <- theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.size = unit(0.5, "lines")
  )

data(anscombe)
al <- data.frame(
  x = c(anscombe$x1, anscombe$x2, anscombe$x3, anscombe$x4),
  y = c(anscombe$y1, anscombe$y2, anscombe$y3, anscombe$y4),
  ds = factor(rep(c("I", "II", "III", "IV"), each = 11))
)

p1 <- ggplot(al, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#E74C3C", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#2C3E50", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ds, nrow = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Anscombe's Quartet",
    subtitle = "All four: x̄=9, ȳ≈7.5, r≈0.82, same regression line",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) + t

p1









Every one of these four panels has virtually identical summary numbers. Only by plotting them do you see that dataset II is curved, dataset III has an outlier throwing off an otherwise perfect line, and dataset IV is driven entirely by one extreme x-value.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Regression to the Mean
The idea: Extremely tall parents tend to have children who are tall, but usually a bit closer to average than the parents were. This isn’t because nature is “pulling” people toward average — it happens naturally whenever a trait combines something real and inherited with a random element (luck, measurement noise, etc.). Any time you pick an extreme case, part of how extreme it was is just chance, and chance doesn’t repeat, so the next measurement tends to look more ordinary.


Code
set.seed(42)
n        <- 200
parent   <- rnorm(n, 170, 8)
child    <- 170 + 0.55 * (parent - 170) + rnorm(n, 0, 6)
rtm      <- data.frame(parent, child)

# Classify parents as short / average / tall for coloring
rtm$cat <- cut(rtm$parent,
               breaks = quantile(rtm$parent, c(0, .2, .8, 1)),
               labels = c("Short parents", "Average", "Tall parents"),
               include.lowest = TRUE)

p2 <- ggplot(rtm, aes(parent, child, color = cat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(data = rtm, aes(parent, child), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 154, y = 191,
           label = "slope = 1\n(no regression)", size = 2.9,
           color = "grey50", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 183, y = 164,
           label = "actual slope\n< 1", size = 2.9,
           color = "#E74C3C", hjust = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Short parents" = "#3498DB",
               "Average"       = "grey70",
               "Tall parents"  = "#9B59B6"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Regression to the Mean",
    subtitle = "Tall parents' children are shorter than them; short parents' children are taller",
    x = "Parent height (cm)", y = "Child height (cm)"
  ) + theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
        legend.position = "bottom")

p2









If there were no regression effect, the red best-fit line would follow the dashed “slope = 1” line exactly. Instead it’s flatter — tall parents’ children land closer to average, and short parents’ children do too.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Will Rogers Phenomenon
The idea: Named after a joke by comedian Will Rogers about migration between US states, this shows that moving a single data point from one group to another can raise the average of both groups — even though no individual value actually changed. This happens when the moved value is below the average of the group it’s leaving, but above the average of the group it’s joining.


Code
a_before <- c(6, 8, 9, 10, 12)   # mean = 9.0
b_before <- c(1, 2, 3, 4,  5)   # mean = 3.0
# Move 6 from A -> B:  new mean A = 9.75 (+0.75),  new mean B = 3.5 (+0.5)
a_after  <- c(8, 9, 10, 12)
b_after  <- c(1, 2,  3,  4,  5, 6)

make_wr <- function(vals, group, timing, moved_val = NULL) {
  data.frame(
    value  = vals,
    group  = group,
    timing = timing,
    moved  = if (!is.null(moved_val)) vals == moved_val else FALSE
  )
}

wr <- rbind(
  make_wr(a_before, "Group A", "Before", 6),
  make_wr(b_before, "Group B", "Before"),
  make_wr(a_after,  "Group A", "After"),
  make_wr(b_after,  "Group B", "After", 6)
)
wr$timing <- factor(wr$timing, levels = c("Before", "After"))

wr_means <- aggregate(value ~ group + timing, wr, mean)

p3 <- ggplot(wr, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = moved), width = 0.09, size = 3.2, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_crossbar(data = wr_means, aes(y = value, ymin = value, ymax = value),
                width = 0.45, color = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = wr_means,
            aes(y = value, label = paste0("μ = ", round(value, 2))),
            vjust = -0.7, size = 2.9, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~timing) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "#3498DB", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"),
    labels = c("Stationary", "Moved (value = 6)"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Will Rogers Phenomenon",
    subtitle = "Moving one value from A to B raises the average of BOTH groups",
    x = NULL, y = "Value"
  ) + theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
        legend.position = "bottom")

p3









The value “6” (highlighted in red) starts out below Group A’s average of 9, dragging it down. Once moved to Group B, it’s above B’s average of 3, pulling that average up too. Result: both group averages rise, purely from reclassification — nothing about the underlying data changed. This is a real concern in medicine, e.g. when improved diagnostics move borderline patients into a more severe category, apparently improving survival rates in both categories.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Berkson’s Paradox
The idea: Two traits can be completely unrelated in the general population, yet appear negatively correlated once you only look at a selected subgroup. Classic example: talent and hard work might be independent among all applicants to a competitive program, but among the people who actually got admitted, the very talented ones didn’t need to work as hard, and the very hard-working ones didn’t need as much raw talent — because admission itself required a combination of the two. The selection process manufactures a correlation that isn’t really there.


Code
set.seed(42)
n2        <- 600
talent    <- rnorm(n2)
hardwork  <- rnorm(n2)
selected  <- (talent + hardwork) > 0.7

berk <- data.frame(talent, hardwork, selected)

r_all <- round(cor(talent, hardwork), 3)
r_sel <- round(cor(talent[selected], hardwork[selected]), 3)

p4 <- ggplot(berk, aes(talent, hardwork, color = selected)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_smooth(data = berk, aes(talent, hardwork), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "grey40", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(berk, selected), aes(talent, hardwork),
              inherit.aes = FALSE,
              method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "grey75", `TRUE` = "#3498DB"),
    labels = c("Not selected", "Selected"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = -2.8, y = 2.9,
           label = paste0("Overall r = ", r_all, "  (dashed)"),
           hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.8, y = 2.4,
           label = paste0("Selected r = ", r_sel, "  (solid)"),
           hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = "#E74C3C") +
  labs(
    title    = "Berkson's Paradox",
    subtitle = "Talent & hard work are independent — but look negatively correlated among the admitted",
    x = "Talent", y = "Hard Work"
  ) + theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5),
        legend.position = "bottom")

p4









Across everyone (dashed line), talent and hard work have essentially zero relationship. But restrict to just the blue “selected” points, and the solid red trend line slopes clearly downward — an illusion created entirely by the selection cutoff.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
section: Range Restriction: How Narrowing Your Data Kills Correlation
text:
Range Restriction: How Narrowing Your Data Kills Correlation
The idea: If two variables have a genuinely strong relationship, but you only ever look at a narrow slice of one variable’s range, the correlation you measure can look weak or even vanish — not because the relationship changed, but because you’re only seeing a thin cross-section of it. This matters anywhere data gets filtered before analysis, e.g. studying only applicants who passed a screening test, or only patients who came back for a follow-up.

Panel 1 — The Full Picture


Code
set.seed(7)
n <- 400

# True relationship: x and y with r ~ 0.80
x   <- rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 15)
eps <- rnorm(n, sd = 15 * sqrt(1 - 0.80^2))
y   <- 0.80 * x + eps

dat       <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
r_full    <- cor(x, y)

lo <- 42; hi <- 58
dat$selected <- x >= lo & x <= hi
r_sub <- cor(x[dat$selected], y[dat$selected])

t <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5)
  )

p1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3498DB", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, fill = "#3498DB",
              color = "#2471A3", linewidth = 1.1, alpha = 0.15) +
  annotate("label", x = 18, y = max(y) * 0.97,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(r_full, 2)),
           size = 4, fontface = "bold", color = "#2471A3",
           fill = "white", label.size = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "Full sample  (n = 400)",
    subtitle = "Strong, clearly visible correlation",
    x = "Score (X)", y = "Outcome (Y)"
  ) + t

p1









With the full range of X visible, the strong upward relationship (r ≈ 0.80) is obvious.


Panel 2 — Zooming Into a Narrow Window


Code
p2 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
  # shade the selected window
  annotate("rect", xmin = lo, xmax = hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.07) +
  # grey out out-of-range points
  geom_point(data = subset(dat, !selected),
             color = "grey80", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.4) +
  # highlight in-range points
  geom_point(data = subset(dat, selected),
             color = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.75, size = 1.8) +
  # full-sample regression (ghost)
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "#3498DB", linewidth = 0.8,
              linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.6) +
  # subsample regression
  geom_smooth(data = subset(dat, selected), method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              fill = "#E74C3C", color = "#C0392B",
              linewidth = 1.1, alpha = 0.18) +
  # boundary markers
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lo, hi), linetype = "dotted",
             color = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("label", x = (lo + hi) / 2, y = max(y) * 0.97,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(r_sub, 2), "\n(subsample)"),
           size = 3.6, fontface = "bold", color = "#C0392B",
           fill = "white", label.size = 0, vjust = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = 18, y = max(y) * 0.97,
           label = paste0("r = ", round(r_full, 2), "\n(full)"),
           size = 3.2, color = "grey55", fill = "white",
           label.size = 0, vjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = (lo + hi) / 2, y = min(y) + 2,
           label = paste0("[", lo, " – ", hi, "]"),
           size = 3, color = "#C0392B") +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("Subsample: x ∈ [", lo, ", ", hi, "]  (n = ",
                      sum(dat$selected), ")"),
    subtitle = "Same data, narrower window — correlation collapses",
    x = "Score (X)", y = "Outcome (Y)"
  ) + t

p2









Same underlying dataset — we’ve just zoomed into the red-shaded window of X values. The correlation inside that window drops sharply from 0.8 to about 0.26, even though nothing about the true relationship changed.


Panel 3 — Correlation as a Function of Window Width


Code
half_widths <- seq(4, 44, by = 2)
curve_dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(half_widths, function(hw) {
  sub <- dat[abs(dat$x - 50) < hw, ]
  data.frame(
    window_width = hw * 2,
    r            = if (nrow(sub) >= 10) cor(sub$x, sub$y) else NA,
    n_sub        = nrow(sub)
  )
}))
curve_dat <- curve_dat[!is.na(curve_dat$r), ]

used_width <- hi - lo

p3 <- ggplot(curve_dat, aes(window_width, r)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = r_full, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#3498DB", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(color = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(color = "#E74C3C", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = used_width, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = curve_dat[curve_dat$window_width == used_width, ],
             size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "#E74C3C", color = "black", stroke = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = used_width + 1.5, y = 0.12,
           label = paste0("panel 2\n(width=", used_width, ")"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "#C0392B") +
  annotate("text", x = max(curve_dat$window_width) - 1,
           y = r_full + 0.025,
           label = paste0("true r = ", round(r_full, 2)),
           hjust = 1, size = 3.2, color = "#3498DB") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Observed r vs. Range Width",
    subtitle = "Narrowing the observed range shrinks the observed correlation",
    x = "Width of observed x-window",
    y = "Observed Pearson r"
  ) + t

p3









This traces out exactly how much correlation you’d measure for every possible window width. The dashed blue line marks the “true” correlation from the full data; the red curve shows how far below that you land the more you restrict your range. The circled point marks the specific narrow window used in Panel 2.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Birthday Paradox
The idea: How many people need to be in a room before there’s a better-than-50% chance that two of them share a birthday? Most people guess somewhere near 180 (half of 365). The real answer is just 23. The trick is that you’re not comparing one person against everyone else — you’re comparing every pair of people, and the number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people.


Code
C1 <- "#E74C3C"; C2 <- "#3498DB"; C3 <- "#27AE60"
C4 <- "#9B59B6"; C5 <- "#F39C12"; CG <- "grey55"

t <- theme_bw(base_size = 13) + theme(
  plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
  plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 8.5, lineheight = 1.2),
  legend.position = "bottom",
  legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "lines"),
  legend.text     = element_text(size = 8)
)

bd <- data.frame(n = 1:70)
bd$prob <- sapply(bd$n, function(n) 1 - prod((365:(365 - n + 1)) / 365))

p1 <- ggplot(bd, aes(n, prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = prob), fill = C2, alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(color = C2, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = CG) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 23, linetype = "dotted", color = C1) +
  geom_point(data = bd[bd$n == 23, ], size = 3.5,
             shape = 21, fill = "white", color = C1, stroke = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 26, y = 0.36, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C1,
           label = "n = 23\np > 50%") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%"),
                     limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Birthday Paradox",
       subtitle = "P(≥2 shared birthdays) by group size",
       x = "People in group", y = "Probability") + t

p1









The probability curve crosses 50% at just 23 people, and by around 70 people it’s essentially guaranteed. Pairwise comparisons scale much faster than intuition expects.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
False Positive Paradox (Base Rate Fallacy)
The idea: Even a highly accurate medical test can be wrong about you as often as it’s right, or more often, if the condition it’s testing for is rare. If a test is 99% accurate (both at correctly flagging sick people and correctly clearing healthy ones), but only 1% of the population actually has the disease, roughly half of all positive results will still be false alarms. Rarity, not test quality, is what dominates here.


Code
prev_seq <- seq(0.001, 0.30, length.out = 300)
sens <- 0.99; spec <- 0.99
ppv  <- (sens * prev_seq) / (sens * prev_seq + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev_seq))
fp_dat <- data.frame(prev = prev_seq, ppv = ppv)

hit <- fp_dat[which.min(abs(fp_dat$prev - 0.01)), ]

p2 <- ggplot(fp_dat, aes(prev, ppv)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = ppv), fill = C1, alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_line(color = C1, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = CG) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.01, linetype = "dotted", color = C4) +
  geom_point(data = hit, size = 3.5,
             shape = 21, fill = "white", color = C4, stroke = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.014, y = 0.30, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C4,
           label = "1% prevalence\nPPV ≈ 50%!") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x * 100, "%")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%"),
                     limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "False Positive Paradox",
       subtitle = "P(truly sick | positive test)  [sens = spec = 99%]",
       x = "True disease prevalence", y = "Positive predictive value") + t

p2









The y-axis (positive predictive value) is the chance a positive result is a true positive. At 1% prevalence it’s only 50% — a coin flip — even though the test itself is 99% accurate. As the disease becomes more common (moving right), the test becomes far more trustworthy.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Parrondo’s Paradox
The idea: Take two gambling games that are each, individually, rigged to lose money on average. Now switch between them in a fixed pattern (A, B, B, A, B, B, …). Astonishingly, the combined strategy can win over time. This happens because Game B’s odds depend on your current capital (whether it is a multiple of 3), and the moves made in Game A knock your capital out of Game B’s unfavorable state more often than Game B alone would — their interaction creates an opportunity that neither game has on its own.


Code
play_game <- function(game, capital) {
  p <- if (game == "A") 0.495 else if (capital %% 3 == 0) 0.095 else 0.745
  capital + if (runif(1) < p) 1L else -1L
}

run_strat <- function(strategy, rounds = 300) {
  cap <- 0L
  sapply(seq_len(rounds), function(i) {
    g <- if (strategy == "A") "A"
    else if (strategy == "B") "B"
    else if (i %% 3 == 1) "A" else "B"   # repeating A, B, B pattern
    cap <<- play_game(g, cap)
    cap
  })
}

n_sims <- 40
par_dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("A", "B", "A+B (ABB pattern)"), function(strat) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_sims), function(s) {
    set.seed(s * 17)
    data.frame(round = seq_len(300), capital = run_strat(strat),
               sim = s, strategy = strat)
  }))
}))
par_mean <- aggregate(capital ~ round + strategy, par_dat, mean)
end_cap  <- with(par_mean[par_mean$round == 300, ], setNames(capital, strategy))

p3 <- ggplot(par_dat, aes(round, capital,
                          group = interaction(sim, strategy), color = strategy)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.07, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = par_mean, aes(group = strategy), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("A" = C1, "B" = CG, "A+B (ABB pattern)" = C3),
    labels = c("A" = "Game A  (losing)", "B" = "Game B  (losing)",
               "A+B (ABB pattern)" = "Switching A,B,B  (winning!)")
  ) +
  labs(title = "Parrondo's Paradox",
       subtitle = "Two losing games → winning strategy when played in an A,B,B pattern",
       x = "Round", y = "Capital", color = NULL) + t

p3









Both Game A (red) and Game B (grey) drift below zero on average — they’re losing propositions on their own (average capital after 300 rounds: -5.35 and -2.6). But playing them in the repeating pattern A, B, B (green) climbs upward, to 16.25 after 300 rounds. Note that simple one-for-one alternation (ABAB) is not enough with these parameters: it still loses slightly. Combining two “bad” strategies can beat either one alone.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Survivorship Bias
The idea: If you only study the winners — the WWII planes that made it back to base, the startups that became famous, the people who “made it” — you get a distorted picture of what actually causes success, because the failures that could tell a different story are invisible to you. Here, “outcome” depends partly on quality and partly on luck, but if we only look at data points that crossed a “survived” threshold, the relationship between quality and outcome is distorted — in this case it is flattened, because low-quality survivors are exactly the ones who got very lucky.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_surv <- 500
quality <- rnorm(n_surv, 50, 12)
luck    <- rnorm(n_surv, 0, 18)
outcome <- 0.3 * quality + luck + 20
sv_dat  <- data.frame(quality, outcome, survived = outcome > 55)
b_all   <- coef(lm(outcome ~ quality, sv_dat))[[2]]
b_sv    <- coef(lm(outcome ~ quality, subset(sv_dat, survived)))[[2]]

p4 <- ggplot(sv_dat, aes(quality, outcome)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(sv_dat, !survived),
             color = "grey82", size = 1.3, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = subset(sv_dat, survived),
             color = C2, size = 1.6, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = CG,
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(sv_dat, survived),
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = C2, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 55, linetype = "dotted", color = C1, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 17, y = 57.5, hjust = 0, size = 2.7, color = C1,
           label = "success threshold") +
  annotate("text", x = 74, y = 22,  hjust = 1, size = 2.7, color = "grey60",
           label = "unseen failures") +
  annotate("text", x = 74, y = 84,  hjust = 1, size = 2.7, color = C2,
           label = "observed survivors") +
  labs(title = "Survivorship Bias",
       subtitle = "Survivors (blue) give a distorted view of how quality relates to outcome",
       x = "Quality", y = "Outcome") + t

p4









Looking only at the blue “survivors,” quality barely seems to matter (the solid blue line is nearly flat, slope ≈ 0.13). Across everyone, including the grey failures, the true slope (dashed line) is more than twice as steep (≈ 0.29). Judging only by survivors gives a distorted picture: their outcomes are inflated by luck, which hides how quality really relates to outcome.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Inspection Paradox
The idea: If buses arrive randomly with an average gap of 10 minutes between them, and you show up at a random moment, your expected wait is not 5 minutes (half the average gap) but the full 10 minutes, because the gap you land in averages about 20 minutes. Why? Because you’re more likely to arrive during a long gap than a short one — long gaps simply take up more clock time, so they’re easier to “land in.” This is why your personal experience of waiting always seems worse than the average would suggest.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_gaps  <- 4000
gap_all <- rexp(n_gaps, rate = 1 / 10)
gap_hit <- sample(gap_all, n_gaps, replace = TRUE, prob = gap_all / sum(gap_all))

insp_dat <- data.frame(
  gap    = c(gap_all, gap_hit),
  source = rep(c(paste0("All gaps  (mean = ", round(mean(gap_all), 1), " min)"),
                 paste0("Gap you land in  (mean = ", round(mean(gap_hit), 1), " min)")),
               each = n_gaps)
)

p5 <- ggplot(insp_dat, aes(gap, fill = source, color = source)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.30, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(gap_all)), color = C2,
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(gap_hit)), color = C1,
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(gap_all) + 1, y = 0.068,
           label = paste0(round(mean(gap_all), 1), " min"), hjust = 0,
           size = 2.8, color = C2) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(gap_hit) + 1, y = 0.068,
           label = paste0(round(mean(gap_hit), 1), " min"), hjust = 0,
           size = 2.8, color = C1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 60)) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c(C2, C1), name = NULL) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(C2, C1), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Inspection Paradox",
       subtitle = "You always seem to arrive mid-gap — because longer gaps are easier to land in",
       x = "Gap length (min)", y = "Density") + t

p5









The blue curve is the true distribution of gaps between buses (mean ≈ 10.2 minutes). The red curve is the distribution of gaps that a random arrival actually experiences (mean ≈ 20.5 minutes, about double) — shifted noticeably to the right, because random arrivals are “size-biased” toward longer gaps.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Accuracy Paradox
The idea: When one outcome is much more common than the other (e.g. most patients are healthy), a model can score very high “accuracy” while being completely useless. A model that always predicts “healthy” will be right 95% of the time if 95% of patients truly are healthy — while catching exactly zero of the actual sick patients. Accuracy alone can hide a model that provides no real value; you need to also look at recall (how many true cases it actually catches).


Code
make_cm <- function(tp, fp, tn, fn, model_label) {
  total <- tp + fp + tn + fn
  data.frame(
    actual    = factor(c("Sick","Sick","Healthy","Healthy"),
                       levels = c("Sick","Healthy")),
    predicted = factor(c("Sick","Healthy","Sick","Healthy"),
                       levels = c("Sick","Healthy")),
    pct       = round(c(tp, fn, fp, tn) / total * 100, 1),
    model     = model_label
  )
}

acc_dat <- rbind(
  make_cm(0, 0, 9500, 500,
          "Model A  ('always Healthy')\nAccuracy 95%  |  Recall 0%"),
  make_cm(400, 900, 8600, 100,
          "Model B  (real classifier)\nAccuracy 90%  |  Recall 80%")
)

p6 <- ggplot(acc_dat, aes(predicted, actual, fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(pct, "%")), size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "white", mid = "#FFF3B0",
                       high = C1, midpoint = 30,
                       name = "% of total") +
  labs(title = "Accuracy Paradox",
       subtitle = "95%-accurate model catches zero sick patients",
       x = "Predicted", y = "Actual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "grey45", size = 10),
        strip.text      = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "none")

p6









Model A boasts 95% accuracy but its “Sick / Predicted Sick” cell is 0% — it never identifies a single sick patient. Model B has lower accuracy (90%) but is actually useful, correctly flagging 80% of sick patients. Never judge a classifier by accuracy alone when classes are imbalanced.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Friendship Paradox
The idea: On average, your friends have more friends than you do. This isn’t a comment on your popularity — it’s a mathematical property of networks. Highly-connected people show up in many people’s friend lists, so when you average “how many friends does my friend have,” those popular people get counted repeatedly and pull the average up.


Code
edges_fp <- data.frame(
  a = c(1,1,1,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4,5,6,7,8),
  b = c(2,3,4,5,6,7,3,8,9,10,9,10,11,11,12)
)
all_n <- 1:12
deg   <- sapply(all_n, function(v) sum(edges_fp$a == v | edges_fp$b == v))

fp_dat <- data.frame(
  own = deg,
  mean_nbr = sapply(all_n, function(v) {
    nb <- union(edges_fp$b[edges_fp$a == v], edges_fp$a[edges_fp$b == v])
    if (!length(nb)) return(NA)
    mean(deg[nb])
  })
)
fp_dat <- na.omit(fp_dat)

p7 <- ggplot(fp_dat, aes(own, mean_nbr)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
              color = CG, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(color = C4, size = 3.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.1, y = 5.5, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C4,
           label = "above the line:\nyour friends have\nmore friends than you") +
  labs(title = "Friendship Paradox",
       subtitle = "Mean neighbor degree > own degree for most nodes",
       x = "Your degree (# friends)",
       y = "Mean degree of your friends") + t

p7









Most points (8 of 12 people; several overlap) sit above the dashed diagonal line, meaning their friends have more connections than they do. Only the two most-connected people (degree 4 and 6, at the far right) fall below it, and two people sit exactly on it.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Braess’s Paradox
The idea: Adding a brand-new, free shortcut to a road network can make traffic worse for everyone. This happens because every driver selfishly picks whatever looks like the fastest route for themselves; once the new road exists, enough drivers pile onto it that it creates a new bottleneck, and the system settles into a “Nash equilibrium” where everyone’s total travel time is higher than before the shortcut existed.


Code
nodes_b <- data.frame(x = c(0,2,2,4), y = c(1,2,0,1), lbl = c("S","A","B","T"))

segs_before <- data.frame(
  x=c(0,2,0,2), y=c(1,2,1,0), xend=c(2,4,2,4), yend=c(2,1,0,1),
  cost=c("x/N","1","1","x/N"), new=FALSE
)
segs_after <- rbind(segs_before,
                    data.frame(x=2,y=2,xend=2,yend=0,cost="0  ← new!",new=TRUE)
)

make_net <- function(segs, nodes, title_str, cost_str, cost_col) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = segs,
                 aes(x,y,xend=xend,yend=yend,color=new,linewidth=new),
                 arrow = arrow(length=unit(0.18,"cm"),type="closed")) +
    geom_label(data = segs,
               aes((x+xend)/2 + ifelse(cost=="0  ← new!", 0.22, 0),
                   (y+yend)/2 + ifelse(cost=="0  ← new!", 0, 0),
                   label=cost, color=new),
               size=2.7, label.size=0, fill="white") +
    geom_point(data=nodes, aes(x,y), size=9, color="#2C3E50") +
    geom_text(data=nodes, aes(x,y,label=lbl),
              color="white", fontface="bold", size=3.5) +
    annotate("text", x=2, y=-0.35, label=cost_str, hjust=0.5,
             size=3.2, fontface="bold", color=cost_col) +
    scale_color_manual(values=c(`FALSE`="grey40",`TRUE`=C1), guide="none") +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values=c(`FALSE`=0.8,`TRUE`=1.4), guide="none") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-0.5, 2.5)) +
    labs(subtitle=title_str) +
    theme_void(base_size=10) +
    theme(plot.subtitle=element_text(color="grey40",size=8,hjust=0.5))
}

net1 <- make_net(segs_before, nodes_b, "Without new road", "Nash cost = 1.5", C3)
net2 <- make_net(segs_after,  nodes_b, "With free A→B road (red)", "Nash cost = 2.0  ↑", C1)

p8 <- (net1 / net2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Braess's Paradox",
    subtitle = "Adding a free road raises everyone's travel time at equilibrium",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face="bold", size=13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color="grey45", size=9)
    )
  )

p8









In the top network, drivers split evenly between the two routes (S→A→T and S→B→T), each taking 1.5 units of time. Once the free A→B shortcut is added (bottom), it becomes individually rational for everyone to route through it — but that congests the shared x/N segments, and the equilibrium travel time rises to 2.0 for everyone. More capacity, worse outcome — because no single driver has an incentive to avoid the “shortcut” unilaterally.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
P-hacking / Multiple Comparisons
The idea: If you run 100 statistical tests on data that has no real effect at all, roughly 5 of them will still come out “statistically significant” purely by chance, if you use the standard 5% significance threshold. This is exactly what that threshold means: a 5% chance of a false alarm on any single test. Run enough tests and cherry-pick the “significant” ones without accounting for how many tests you ran, and you’ll “discover” effects that are pure noise. This is a major reason many published findings fail to replicate.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_tests <- 100
pv      <- sort(runif(n_tests))
ph_dat  <- data.frame(rank = seq_len(n_tests), p = pv, sig = pv < 0.05)

p9 <- ggplot(ph_dat, aes(rank, p, fill = sig, color = sig)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, color = C1, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c(`TRUE` = C1, `FALSE` = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = C1, `FALSE` = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = 0.11, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, color = C1,
           label = paste0(sum(ph_dat$sig), " 'significant' results\n(all truly null!)")) +
  labs(title = "P-hacking / Multiple Comparisons",
       subtitle = paste0("100 tests on pure noise — about 5 expected to cross α=0.05 by chance (",
                         sum(ph_dat$sig), " here)"),
       x = "Test (sorted by p-value)", y = "p-value") + t

p9









None of these 100 tests reflect a real effect — the underlying data was pure random noise. Yet a handful of bars dip below the red 0.05 threshold purely by chance, and in a real analysis those would be the ones that get reported as “significant findings” if you didn’t correct for the number of tests run.

title: A Gallery of Statistical Paradoxes
text:
Takeaway
Every one of these graphs shows the same underlying warning: statistics computed on data can mislead you unless you understand how the data was grouped, selected, filtered, or compared. Aggregation, selection bias, imbalanced classes, restricted ranges, and repeated testing can all make a relationship appear, disappear, or reverse — without any single number “lying” on its own. The fix is always the same: look at the full picture, plot your data, and think carefully about how it was collected before trusting a summary statistic.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
text:
A female lawyer loses a promotion to a less qualified male colleague. In one version of the story she protests the decision; in the other she accepts it. Do people like her more or less when she protests?
Garcia, Schmitt, Branscombe and Ellemers (2010) asked 129 women to read one of the versions, chosen at random, and to rate how much they liked the lawyer. Two other questions make the data interesting:

When does protesting pay off? The answer may depend on who is judging: on how common the reader believes sex discrimination to be. That is a question of moderation.
Why does protesting change how much she is liked? Perhaps because readers judge protest to be an appropriate response, and like people who respond appropriately. That is a question of mediation.










Moderation
Mediation




Question
When, or for whom, does X affect Y?
How, or why, does X affect Y?


The third variable
A moderator W changes the size or direction of the effect of X
A mediator M carries the effect: X changes M, and M changes Y


In a model
An interaction X × W
Two regressions and the product of two paths, \(a \times b\)


Here
Does the effect of protest depend on perceived sexism?
Does protest raise liking by making her response seem more appropriate?





Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side
library(boot)       # bootstrap confidence intervals
library(lavaan)     # the mediation model as a path model




Code
# a path diagram: boxes, arrows between them, and labels on the arrows
draw_paths <- function(boxes, arrows, title, subtitle = NULL) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_label(data = boxes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.6, fill = "white",
               label.padding = unit(0.45, "lines"), lineheight = 0.9) +
    geom_text(data = arrows, aes(lx, ly, label = label), size = 3.8, colour = "#E74C3C", fontface = "bold") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0.5, 6)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle)
}
moderation <- draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Perceived sexism\n(W)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.7, 5), y = c(1.5, 4.5), xend = c(7.3, 5), yend = c(1.5, 1.6),
                      label = c("", ""), lx = 0, ly = 0),
  title = "Moderation", subtitle = "W changes the effect of X on Y")
mediation <- draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Appropriateness\n(M)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.1, 6.4, 2.7), y = c(2.2, 4.6, 1.5), xend = c(3.7, 7.9, 7.3), yend = c(4.6, 2.2, 1.5),
                      label = c("a", "b", "c′"), lx = c(2.4, 7.6, 5), ly = c(3.6, 3.6, 1.0)),
  title = "Mediation", subtitle = "X affects Y through M (a × b), and directly (c′)")
moderation + mediation









Both use real data: the Garcia data set of the psych package (data("GSBE", package = "psych")), the same data Hayes (2022) uses in his book on these methods.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
text:
1. The data


Code
data("GSBE", package = "psych")       # loads the data frame Garcia
d <- data.frame(protest  = Garcia$prot2,      # 0 = she did not protest, 1 = she protested
                sexism   = Garcia$sexism,     # how pervasive the reader believes sex discrimination is (1-7)
                respappr = Garcia$respappr,   # how appropriate the reader found her response (1-7)
                liking   = Garcia$liking)     # how much the reader liked her (1-7)
table(protest = d$protest)


protest
 0  1 
41 88 


Code
round(aggregate(cbind(sexism, respappr, liking) ~ protest, data = d, FUN = mean), 2)


  protest sexism respappr liking
1       0   5.07     3.88   5.31
2       1   5.14     5.32   5.79


Code
round(sapply(d, sd), 2)


 protest   sexism respappr   liking 
    0.47     0.78     1.35     1.05 










Variable
Role
Meaning




protest
X
0 = the lawyer accepted the decision (41 readers), 1 = she protested (88 readers; the original study had two kinds of protest, combined here)


sexism
W, the moderator
The reader’s belief that sex discrimination is pervasive in society, 1 to 7


respappr
M, the mediator
How appropriate the reader found the lawyer’s response, 1 to 7


liking
Y
How much the reader liked the lawyer, 1 to 7



On average the lawyer who protested was liked a little more (5.79 against 5.31) and her response was judged much more appropriate (5.32 against 3.88). Because the version of the story was assigned at random, the two groups do not differ in perceived sexism.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
section: 2. Moderation: does the effect of protest depend on perceived sexism?
text:
2. Moderation: does the effect of protest depend on perceived sexism?

The model
Moderation is an interaction: we add the product of X and W to the regression.
\[\text{liking} = b_0 + b_1\,\text{protest} + b_2\,\text{sexism} + b_3\,(\text{protest} \times \text{sexism}) + e\]
Rearranging shows what \(b_3\) does. The effect of protest is no longer one number; it is a line that depends on sexism:
\[\text{effect of protest} = \theta(\text{sexism}) = b_1 + b_3 \times \text{sexism}\]
If \(b_3 = 0\), protest has the same effect for every reader. If \(b_3 > 0\), protest helps more the more pervasive the reader believes discrimination to be.


Mean-centre the moderator first
In the equation above, \(b_1\) is the effect of protest when sexism is 0. But sexism runs from 1 to 7, so “sexism = 0” is a reader who does not exist. Subtracting the mean first (mean-centring) makes 0 mean “a reader of average sexism”:


Code
d$sexism_c <- d$sexism - mean(d$sexism)   # 0 = average perceived sexism
fit_raw <- lm(liking ~ protest * sexism,   data = d)
fit_mod <- lm(liking ~ protest * sexism_c, data = d)   # protest * sexism_c = protest + sexism_c + protest:sexism_c
round(rbind(uncentred = coef(fit_raw), centred = coef(fit_mod)), 3)


          (Intercept) protest sexism protest:sexism
uncentred       7.706  -3.773 -0.472          0.834
centred         5.289   0.493 -0.472          0.834



The interaction (0.834) is the same in both models, with the same test, and so are the fit and every prediction.
The protest coefficient changes meaning. Uncentred, -3.77 is the effect of protest for an impossible reader with sexism 0. Centred, 0.49 is the effect for a reader of average sexism.

You may read that centring is needed to “avoid multicollinearity” between X and X × W. It lowers that correlation, but it changes nothing in the test of the interaction (Echambadi & Hess, 2007). Centre for interpretation.


Code
summary(fit_mod)



Call:
lm(formula = liking ~ protest * sexism_c, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.9894 -0.6381  0.0478  0.7404  2.3650 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        5.2885     0.1547  34.184  < 2e-16 ***
protest            0.4926     0.1872   2.631  0.00958 ** 
sexism_c          -0.4725     0.2038  -2.318  0.02205 *  
protest:sexism_c   0.8336     0.2436   3.422  0.00084 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9888 on 125 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1335,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1127 
F-statistic: 6.419 on 3 and 125 DF,  p-value: 0.0004439




How to read the output







Row
Meaning here




(Intercept)
Predicted liking when protest = 0 and sexism is average: 5.29


protest
The effect of protest for a reader of average sexism: 0.49 points more liking


sexism_c
The effect of sexism when she did not protest (protest = 0): readers who see more discrimination like the non-protesting lawyer less


protest:sexism_c
How much the effect of protest grows for each point of sexism: 0.83. This is the moderation test



With an interaction in the model, the “main effects” are conditional effects: each is the effect of one variable when the other is 0. That is why centring matters.


Moderation as a ΔR² step
The interaction can also be tested as one more step of a hierarchical regression: first the two predictors, then their product.


Code
fit_main <- lm(liking ~ protest + sexism_c, data = d)
anova(fit_main, fit_mod)


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: liking ~ protest + sexism_c
Model 2: liking ~ protest * sexism_c
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    126 133.66                                  
2    125 122.21  1    11.451 11.713 0.0008396 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
c(R2_main_effects = summary(fit_main)$r.squared, R2_with_interaction = summary(fit_mod)$r.squared,
  delta_R2 = summary(fit_mod)$r.squared - summary(fit_main)$r.squared,
  t_squared = unname(coef(summary(fit_mod))["protest:sexism_c", "t value"]^2))


    R2_main_effects R2_with_interaction            delta_R2           t_squared 
         0.05229818          0.13349060          0.08119242         11.71256985 


The interaction adds 8.1% of explained variance. The F-change is the square of the interaction’s t: for one added term the two tests are the same test.


Simple slopes: the effect of protest at chosen levels of sexism
The conditional effect of protest at a value \(w\) of (centred) sexism is \(\theta(w) = b_1 + b_3 w\). Its standard error comes from the variances and the covariance of the two coefficients, all in vcov(fit_mod):
\[SE[\theta(w)] = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(b_1) + w^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_3) + 2w \operatorname{Cov}(b_1, b_3)}\]
A common choice is to probe at one SD below the mean, the mean, and one SD above (Aiken & West, 1991):


Code
b <- coef(fit_mod); V <- vcov(fit_mod)
w <- c(-1, 0, 1) * sd(d$sexism)                                 # centred values: -1 SD, mean, +1 SD
theta <- b["protest"] + b["protest:sexism_c"] * w
se    <- sqrt(V["protest", "protest"] + w^2 * V["protest:sexism_c", "protest:sexism_c"] +
              2 * w * V["protest", "protest:sexism_c"])
df_res <- df.residual(fit_mod)
slopes <- data.frame(level = c("-1 SD", "mean", "+1 SD"), sexism = w + mean(d$sexism),
                     effect = theta, se = se, t = theta / se, p = 2 * pt(-abs(theta / se), df_res),
                     lower = theta - qt(.975, df_res) * se, upper = theta + qt(.975, df_res) * se)
slopes[, -1] <- round(slopes[, -1], 3)
slopes


  level sexism effect    se      t     p  lower upper
1 -1 SD  4.333 -0.161 0.263 -0.611 0.542 -0.681 0.360
2  mean  5.117  0.493 0.187  2.631 0.010  0.122 0.863
3 +1 SD  5.901  1.146 0.272  4.216 0.000  0.608 1.684



For readers who see little discrimination (sexism 4.33), protest makes no difference (-0.16, p = 0.54).
For readers who see a lot (sexism 5.90), the lawyer who protests is liked 1.15 points more.

A check: centring sexism at a chosen value turns the protest coefficient into the simple slope at that value, with the same standard error.


Code
fit_high <- lm(liking ~ protest * I(sexism - (mean(sexism) + sd(sexism))), data = d)
coef(summary(fit_high))["protest", ]


    Estimate   Std. Error      t value     Pr(>|t|) 
1.145923e+00 2.718268e-01 4.215637e+00 4.736022e-05 




Johnson–Neyman: where exactly is the effect significant?
The ±1 SD points are arbitrary. The Johnson–Neyman technique finds the values of the moderator where the effect of protest is just significant: where \(|\theta(w) / SE[\theta(w)]|\) equals the critical t. Squaring both sides gives a quadratic equation in \(w\):
\[\left[b_3^2 - t_{crit}^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_3)\right] w^2 + 2\left[b_1 b_3 - t_{crit}^2 \operatorname{Cov}(b_1, b_3)\right] w + \left[b_1^2 - t_{crit}^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_1)\right] = 0\]


Code
tc <- qt(.975, df_res)
A <- b[4]^2 - tc^2 * V[4, 4]
B <- 2 * (b[2] * b[4] - tc^2 * V[2, 4])
C <- b[2]^2 - tc^2 * V[2, 2]
jn <- sort((-B + c(-1, 1) * sqrt(B^2 - 4 * A * C)) / (2 * A)) + mean(d$sexism)   # back to the 1-7 scale
c(jn_lower = jn[1], jn_upper = jn[2])


jn_lower jn_upper 
3.508712 4.975297

share_below_lower share_above_upper 
       0.01550388        0.55813953 


Protest has a significant positive effect for readers with sexism above 4.98 (56% of the sample), and a significant negative effect below 3.51, a region with only 2 readers, too few to say much about. In between, the effect is not significantly different from 0.

grid_w <- seq(min(d$sexism), max(d$sexism), length.out = 200)

  labs(title = "The effect of protest on liking, at each level of perceived sexism",
       x = "perceived pervasiveness of sex discrimination (W)",
       y = "effect of protest (95% CI)")









Where the blue band does not include 0, the effect is significant. The dashed lines are the Johnson–Neyman points, and the ticks at the bottom show the readers’ actual sexism scores (one tick per reader, spread a little where readers share a score): most lie to the right of 4.98.


The interaction plot


Code
pred <- expand.grid(protest = c(0, 1), sexism = grid_w)
pred$sexism_c <- pred$sexism - mean(d$sexism)
pr <- predict(fit_mod, newdata = pred, interval = "confidence")
pred <- cbind(pred, pr)
pred$condition <- factor(pred$protest, labels = c("did not protest", "protested"))
d$condition <- factor(d$protest, labels = c("did not protest", "protested"))
ggplot(pred, aes(sexism, fit, colour = condition, fill = condition)) +
  geom_point(data = d, aes(y = liking), alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +

       x = "perceived pervasiveness of sex discrimination (W)", y = "liking of the lawyer",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The lines cross. Among readers who believe discrimination is rare, the lawyer who stays quiet is liked about as much, or slightly more. Among readers who believe it is everywhere, the protester is liked much more, and the quiet lawyer much less.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
section: 3. Mediation: why does protest change liking?
text:
3. Mediation: why does protest change liking?

The paths
Three regressions describe a simple mediation model:
\[\text{total effect:}\qquad Y = i_1 + c\,X + e_1\]
\[\text{a path:}\qquad M = i_2 + a\,X + e_2\]
\[\text{b and c′ paths:}\qquad Y = i_3 + c'\,X + b\,M + e_3\]

\(a\): how much protest changes the perceived appropriateness of her response.
\(b\): how much appropriateness changes liking, among readers who read the same version.
\(c'\): the direct effect, the effect of protest on liking that does not go through appropriateness.
\(a \times b\): the indirect effect, the part of the effect that does go through it.
\(c\): the total effect. In linear regression it splits exactly: \(c = c' + ab\).



Code
fit_c <- lm(liking ~ protest, data = d)                # total effect c
fit_a <- lm(respappr ~ protest, data = d)              # a path
fit_b <- lm(liking ~ protest + respappr, data = d)     # b and c' paths
a  <- unname(coef(fit_a)["protest"])
bp <- unname(coef(fit_b)["respappr"])
cp <- unname(coef(fit_b)["protest"])
cc <- unname(coef(fit_c)["protest"])
round(c(a = a, b = bp, direct_c_prime = cp, indirect_ab = a * bp, total_c = cc, c_prime_plus_ab = cp + a * bp), 3)


              a               b  direct_c_prime     indirect_ab         total_c c_prime_plus_ab 
          1.440           0.402          -0.101           0.579           0.479           0.479 


Protest raised perceived appropriateness by 1.44 points (a), and each point of appropriateness went with 0.40 points more liking (b). The indirect effect is \(1.44 \times 0.40 = 0.58\). The direct effect is practically 0 (-0.10), so the whole total effect of 0.48 runs through appropriateness.


Why not Baron and Kenny’s steps, or the Sobel test?
For decades mediation was tested with the causal steps of Baron and Kenny (1986): (1) X must affect Y (\(c\) significant), (2) X must affect M (\(a\)), (3) M must affect Y controlling for X (\(b\)), and (4) \(c'\) must be smaller than \(c\) (“full” mediation if \(c'\) is not significant). Today this approach is not recommended (Hayes, 2022; Zhao et al., 2010):

It never tests the indirect effect \(ab\) itself, only its pieces, one at a time.
Step 1 is not needed. An indirect effect can exist without a significant total effect, for example when the direct effect has the opposite sign and cancels it out.
“Full” versus “partial” mediation depends on sample size: with enough data, any \(c'\) becomes significant.

The Sobel test does test \(ab\), dividing it by an approximate standard error, \(\sqrt{b^2 \operatorname{Var}(a) + a^2 \operatorname{Var}(b)}\), and comparing it with the normal distribution. But the product of two estimates is not normally distributed: its sampling distribution is skewed, so symmetric normal intervals are wrong and the test has low power (MacKinnon et al., 2004).


Code
se_sobel <- sqrt(bp^2 * vcov(fit_a)["protest", "protest"] + a^2 * vcov(fit_b)["respappr", "respappr"])
c(z = a * bp / se_sobel, lower = a * bp - 1.96 * se_sobel, upper = a * bp + 1.96 * se_sobel)


        z     lower     upper 
4.3206484 0.3165276 0.8421410 




The bootstrap: the recommended test of the indirect effect
The bootstrap makes no assumption about the shape of the sampling distribution of \(ab\). Draw a new sample of 129 readers with replacement from the data, fit the two regressions, compute \(ab\), and repeat thousands of times. The middle 95% of the \(ab\) values is the percentile bootstrap confidence interval (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). If it does not contain 0, the indirect effect is significant.


Code
indirect <- function(data, i) {
  x <- data[i, ]                                     # one bootstrap sample
  a_i <- coef(lm(respappr ~ protest, data = x))["protest"]
  b_i <- coef(lm(liking ~ protest + respappr, data = x))["respappr"]
  c(ab = unname(a_i * b_i), ab_partially_std = unname(a_i * b_i / sd(x$liking)))
}
set.seed(2026)
boot_ab <- boot(d, indirect, R = 5000)
ci_ab <- quantile(boot_ab$t[, 1], c(.025, .975))
ci_ab


     2.5%     97.5% 
0.3198499 0.9059003 




Code
bd <- data.frame(ab = boot_ab$t[, 1])
xs <- seq(min(bd$ab), max(bd$ab), length.out = 300)
ggplot(bd, aes(ab)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(ab = xs, density = dnorm(xs, a * bp, se_sobel)), aes(y = density),
            colour = "#f39c12", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_ab, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "5,000 bootstrap indirect effects (blue) and the normal curve\nthe Sobel test assumes (orange)",
       x = "indirect effect a × b", y = "density")









The bootstrap distribution is skewed to the right: its interval [0.32, 0.91] reaches further above the estimate (0.58) than below it. The Sobel interval is symmetric by construction. Here both exclude 0, because the effect is large; in smaller samples, or with smaller effects, they can disagree, and the bootstrap is the one to trust.


The same model in lavaan
lavaan fits the two regressions at once as a path model. Labels (a*, b*, cp*) name the paths, and := defines new quantities from them:


Code
model <- '
  respappr ~ a * protest                # a path
  liking   ~ cp * protest + b * respappr  # direct effect and b path
  indirect := a * b
  total    := cp + a * b
'
set.seed(2026)
fit_sem <- sem(model, data = d, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 1000)
pe <- parameterEstimates(fit_sem, boot.ci.type = "perc")
pe[pe$op %in% c("~", ":="), c("label", "lhs", "op", "rhs", "est", "se", "pvalue", "ci.lower", "ci.upper")]


     label      lhs op      rhs    est    se pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1        a respappr  ~  protest  1.440 0.247   0.00    0.952    1.939
2       cp   liking  ~  protest -0.101 0.203   0.62   -0.497    0.297
3        b   liking  ~ respappr  0.402 0.080   0.00    0.246    0.554
7 indirect indirect :=      a*b  0.579 0.153   0.00    0.311    0.896
8    total    total :=   cp+a*b  0.479 0.221   0.03    0.066    0.906



est are the same estimates as from lm().
se are bootstrap standard errors, and ci.lower, ci.upper percentile bootstrap intervals (boot.ci.type = "perc").
We used 1,000 bootstrap samples to keep this page fast; lavaan refits the whole model each time, which is slow. For a report, use 5,000 or more, as with boot() above. With more samples, the interval limits change only in the second decimal.



How big is the indirect effect?
\(ab\) is in the units of the outcome: protest raises liking by 0.58 points of a 1 to 7 scale through appropriateness. Two standardised versions make it comparable across studies (Hayes, 2022):

Partially standardised: \(ab / SD_Y\), the indirect effect in standard deviations of Y. Use it when X is a two-group variable, as here: the groups differ by 0.55 SD of liking through this path.
Completely standardised: \(ab \times SD_X / SD_Y\), for a continuous X: the change in Y, in SDs, for one SD more of X.



Code
ci_ps <- quantile(boot_ab$t[, 2], c(.025, .975))
round(c(partially_standardised = a * bp / sd(d$liking), lower = unname(ci_ps[1]), upper = unname(ci_ps[2])), 3)


partially_standardised                  lower                  upper 
                 0.552                  0.331                  0.826 


Avoid the “proportion mediated” (\(ab / c\)): it is unstable in all but very large samples, and meaningless when \(c\) is small or the paths have opposite signs.


What mediation needs to be causal
A mediation analysis tells a causal story, X → M → Y, and the numbers alone cannot prove it.

X was randomised. Readers were assigned to the versions of the story at random, so the effects of protest, \(a\) and \(c\), are causal.
M was not. Appropriateness was measured, not manipulated. The \(b\) path (and therefore \(c'\) and \(ab\)) is causal only if nothing else affects both appropriateness and liking. A reader’s general sympathy for the lawyer, for example, could raise both, and would make \(b\) too large. This no unmeasured confounding assumption cannot be tested with these data (Imai et al., 2010).
Temporal order. M must come after X and before Y. Here M and Y were measured at the same moment, so “liking makes her response seem appropriate” is also possible.
Cross-sectional data (all variables measured at once, nothing randomised) make mediation estimates especially doubtful when the process unfolds over time (Maxwell & Cole, 2007).

Report mediation as consistent with a mechanism, not as proof of it, unless the design supports the causal claims.


Code
s_a <- coef(summary(fit_a)); s_b <- coef(summary(fit_b))
stars <- function(p) if (p < .001) "***" else if (p < .01) "**" else if (p < .05) "*" else ""
draw_paths(
  boxes  = data.frame(x = c(1.6, 8.4, 5), y = c(1.5, 1.5, 5.2),
                      label = c("Protest\n(X)", "Liking\n(Y)", "Appropriateness\n(M)")),
  arrows = data.frame(x = c(2.1, 6.4, 2.7), y = c(2.2, 4.6, 1.5), xend = c(3.7, 7.9, 7.3), yend = c(4.6, 2.2, 1.5),
                      label = c(sprintf("a = %.2f%s", a, stars(s_a["protest", 4])),
                                sprintf("b = %.2f%s", bp, stars(s_b["respappr", 4])),
                                sprintf("c′ = %.2f%s", cp, stars(s_b["protest", 4]))),
                      lx = c(1.7, 8.3, 5), ly = c(3.6, 3.6, 1.0)),
  title = sprintf("Indirect effect ab = %.2f, 95%% bootstrap CI [%.2f, %.2f]; total effect c = %.2f",
                  a * bp, ci_ab[1], ci_ab[2], cc))

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
section: 4. Moderated mediation: does the indirect effect depend on sexism?
text:
4. Moderated mediation: does the indirect effect depend on sexism?
The two questions can be combined. Section 2 showed that perceived sexism moderates the effect of protest on liking. Perhaps it does so through the mediator: readers who see discrimination everywhere find protest more appropriate. Then the \(a\) path depends on sexism, and so does the indirect effect:
\[M = i_2 + a_1 X + a_2 W + a_3\,XW + e_2, \qquad Y = i_3 + c' X + b M + e_3\]
\[\text{conditional indirect effect} = (a_1 + a_3 W) \times b, \qquad \text{index of moderated mediation} = a_3 \times b\]
The index of moderated mediation (Hayes, 2015) is how much the indirect effect changes per point of W. If its bootstrap interval excludes 0, the indirect effect depends on the moderator. (This is model 7 of Hayes’s PROCESS macro.)


Code
fit_a_mod <- lm(respappr ~ protest * sexism_c, data = d)
coef(summary(fit_a_mod))


                   Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)       3.8598115  0.1790674 21.555078 6.302118e-44
protest           1.4580301  0.2167041  6.728208 5.523771e-10
sexism_c         -0.5290051  0.2358875 -2.242617 2.668359e-02
protest:sexism_c  0.8099844  0.2819135  2.873167 4.776441e-03


Code
w_vals <- c(-1, 0, 1) * sd(d$sexism)
cond_indirect <- function(data, i) {
  x <- data[i, ]
  x$sexism_c <- x$sexism - mean(d$sexism)            # centre at the mean of the original sample
  a_i <- coef(lm(respappr ~ protest * sexism_c, data = x))
  b_i <- coef(lm(liking ~ protest + respappr, data = x))["respappr"]
  c(index = unname(a_i["protest:sexism_c"] * b_i),
    setNames((a_i["protest"] + a_i["protest:sexism_c"] * w_vals) * b_i, c("at_minus_1_SD", "at_mean", "at_plus_1_SD")))
}
set.seed(2026)
boot_mm <- boot(d, cond_indirect, R = 5000)
mm <- data.frame(estimate = boot_mm$t0, t(apply(boot_mm$t, 2, quantile, c(.025, .975))))
names(mm)[2:3] <- c("lower", "upper")
round(mm, 3)


              estimate lower upper
index            0.326 0.034 0.666
at_minus_1_SD    0.331 0.079 0.612
at_mean          0.587 0.329 0.905
at_plus_1_SD     0.842 0.420 1.357



Protest made the response seem more appropriate especially to readers who see discrimination as pervasive (the protest:sexism_c row of the \(a\) model).
The index of moderated mediation is 0.33, 95% CI [0.03, 0.67]: the interval excludes 0, so the indirect effect depends on sexism.
The indirect effect is 0.33 for readers one SD below the mean in sexism and 0.84 for readers one SD above.

In words: protesting is judged more appropriate, and therefore the protester is liked more, mainly by readers who already believe that discrimination is common.

section: 5. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
5. Reporting the results in APA style


Code
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
sm   <- coef(summary(fit_mod)); ci_mod <- confint(fit_mod)
dR2  <- summary(fit_mod)$r.squared - summary(fit_main)$r.squared
F_change <- anova(fit_main, fit_mod)$F[2]


Method (data analysis):

Moderation was tested by regressing liking on protest condition (0 = no protest, 1 = protest), perceived pervasiveness of sex discrimination (mean-centred), and their product, and probed with simple slopes at ±1 SD and the Johnson–Neyman technique. The indirect effect of protest on liking through perceived response appropriateness was estimated with ordinary least squares regression and tested with 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals based on 5,000 resamples. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the boot and lavaan packages.

Results:

The effect of protest on liking depended on perceived sexism, b = 0.83, SE = 0.24, t(125) = 3.42, p < .001, 95% CI [0.35, 1.32], ΔR² = .08, F(1, 125) = 11.71. At low perceived sexism (−1 SD), protest did not affect liking, b = -0.16, p = .542; at high perceived sexism (+1 SD), the lawyer who protested was liked more, b = 1.15, p < .001. The Johnson–Neyman technique showed a significant positive effect of protest for perceived sexism above 4.98 (56% of participants). Protest increased perceived response appropriateness, a = 1.44, p < .001, which in turn predicted liking, b = 0.40, p < .001. The indirect effect was significant, ab = 0.58, 95% CI [0.32, 0.91], partially standardised ab = 0.55, whereas the direct effect was not, c′ = -0.10, p = .616. The indirect effect was moderated by perceived sexism, index of moderated mediation = 0.33, 95% CI [0.03, 0.67].

Points to remember:

For moderation, say how the moderator was centred, report the interaction with its ΔR², and probe it: simple slopes at stated values, or the Johnson–Neyman region.
For mediation, report the \(a\), \(b\), direct and indirect effects, and test the indirect effect with a bootstrap confidence interval, giving the number of resamples. Do not rely on the causal steps or the Sobel test.
State the causal assumptions, and which of the paths the design supports.
Cite R and the packages; citation(), citation("boot") and citation("lavaan") in R give the exact references.

title: Moderation and Mediation in R: When and Why Protesting Pays Off
text:
6. Summary







Moderation
When does X affect Y? lm(y ~ x * w); the interaction \(b_3\) is the test


Centring
Subtract the mean of W so that \(b_1\) is the effect of X at average W; it does not change the interaction test


ΔR²
The interaction as one more step: anova(main_effects, with_interaction); F-change = \(t^2\)


Probing
Simple slopes \(b_1 + b_3 w\) with \(SE = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(b_1) + w^2 \operatorname{Var}(b_3) + 2w \operatorname{Cov}(b_1, b_3)}\); the Johnson–Neyman points where the effect is just significant


Mediation
How does X affect Y? \(a\) from lm(m ~ x), \(b\) and \(c'\) from lm(y ~ x + m); indirect effect \(ab\); \(c = c' + ab\)


Testing \(ab\)
Percentile bootstrap CI (boot(), or lavaan with se = "bootstrap"), not causal steps or Sobel


Effect size
Partially standardised \(ab / SD_Y\) for a two-group X; completely standardised \(ab \cdot SD_X / SD_Y\) for a continuous X


Moderated mediation
A moderated path makes the indirect effect conditional; test with the index of moderated mediation


Causality
Needs randomisation or strong assumptions: no unmeasured confounding of M and Y, and M measured between X and Y
