title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
text:
Suppose 5% of people have a disease and we want to predict who has it from a blood marker, age and smoking. We fit a logistic regression, and a colleague says: “95% zeros and 5% ones? That is a problem, you have to balance the data first.”
It is a very common belief, and it is mostly wrong. The 95/5 split by itself does not hurt logistic regression. What does go wrong is one of four things that often come with a rare outcome:

The 0.5 cutoff (section 3). With a 5% base rate almost nobody gets a predicted probability above 0.5, so the model “predicts” that nobody is sick.
Judging the model by accuracy (section 4). Calling everybody healthy is already 95% accurate.
Too few events (section 5). What limits the model is the number of 1s, not their percentage. With only a handful of them, estimates are unstable and can even run off to infinity.
The popular “fixes” (section 6). Oversampling, undersampling, SMOTE and class weights do not make the model better at telling the groups apart. They make its probabilities wrong.

As a reminder, logistic regression models the probability of a 1:
\[P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots)}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \log\frac{P}{1 - P} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots\]
The slopes \(\beta_1, \beta_2, \dots\) say how the risk changes with each predictor. The intercept \(\beta_0\) sets the overall level of risk, and that is where the 5% lives. Keep this in mind: every “fix” for imbalance in section 6 works by moving the intercept.
As in other pages of this site, we simulate the data, so we know the true answer and can check every method against it.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side
library(pROC)       # ROC curves and the AUC
library(logistf)    # Firth's penalised logistic regression (section 5)

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
text:
Suppose 5% of people have a disease and we want to predict who has it from a blood marker, age and smoking. We fit a logistic regression, and a colleague says: “95% zeros and 5% ones? That is a problem, you have to balance the data first.”
It is a very common belief, and it is mostly wrong. The 95/5 split by itself does not hurt logistic regression. What does go wrong is one of four things that often come with a rare outcome:

The 0.5 cutoff (section 3). With a 5% base rate almost nobody gets a predicted probability above 0.5, so the model “predicts” that nobody is sick.
Judging the model by accuracy (section 4). Calling everybody healthy is already 95% accurate.
Too few events (section 5). What limits the model is the number of 1s, not their percentage. With only a handful of them, estimates are unstable and can even run off to infinity.
The popular “fixes” (section 6). Oversampling, undersampling, SMOTE and class weights do not make the model better at telling the groups apart. They make its probabilities wrong.

As a reminder, logistic regression models the probability of a 1:
\[P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots)}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \log\frac{P}{1 - P} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots\]
The slopes \(\beta_1, \beta_2, \dots\) say how the risk changes with each predictor. The intercept \(\beta_0\) sets the overall level of risk, and that is where the 5% lives. Keep this in mind: every “fix” for imbalance in section 6 works by moving the intercept.
As in other pages of this site, we simulate the data, so we know the true answer and can check every method against it.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side
library(pROC)       # ROC curves and the AUC
library(logistf)    # Firth's penalised logistic regression (section 5)

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
text:
1. Simulate the data
The true model, on the log-odds scale:
\[\log\frac{P(\text{disease})}{1 - P(\text{disease})} = -3.61 + 1.0 \times \text{marker} + 0.5 \times \text{age10} + 1.0 \times \text{smoker}\]

marker: a blood marker in standard deviations. One SD more multiplies the odds of disease by \(e^{1} = 2.72\).
age10: age in decades from 50 (so 1 means 60 years old). Each decade multiplies the odds by \(e^{0.5} = 1.65\).
smoker: 1 for the 10% of people who smoke. Smoking multiplies the odds by \(e^{1} = 2.72\).
The intercept \(-3.61\) was chosen so that 5% of people have the disease.



Code
b_true <- c("(Intercept)" = -3.61, marker = 1.0, age10 = 0.5, smoker = 1.0)

simulate_people <- function(n) {
  marker <- rnorm(n)                  # blood marker, in standard deviations
  age10  <- rnorm(n)                  # age in decades from 50
  smoker <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.10)        # 10% smoke
  log_odds <- b_true[1] + b_true[2] * marker + b_true[3] * age10 + b_true[4] * smoker
  data.frame(disease = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(log_odds)), marker, age10, smoker)
}

set.seed(2026)
test  <- simulate_people(100000)   # "the future": new people we will judge the models on
train <- simulate_people(20000)    # the data we fit the models to

c(people = nrow(train), sick = sum(train$disease), share_sick = mean(train$disease))


    people       sick share_sick 
 2.000e+04  9.550e+02  4.775e-02 


plogis() turns log-odds into a probability: \(\text{plogis}(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{-z})\). So rbinom(n, 1, plogis(log_odds)) gives each person the disease with their own probability.
The training data has 955 sick people out of 20,000: a 95/5 split. In real life we never have a test set of 100,000 new people. Section 7 shows how to do without one.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
section: 2. A large sample: the model is fine
text:
2. A large sample: the model is fine


Code
fit <- glm(disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, family = binomial, data = train)
summary(fit)



Call:
glm(formula = disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, family = binomial, 
    data = train)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept) -3.70687    0.05269  -70.36   <2e-16 ***
marker       1.04643    0.03767   27.78   <2e-16 ***
age10        0.49340    0.03557   13.87   <2e-16 ***
smoker       1.07257    0.08818   12.16   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 7673.4  on 19999  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 6500.2  on 19996  degrees of freedom
AIC: 6508.2

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 7



How to read the output







Column
Meaning




Estimate
The change in the log-odds of disease for one unit more of the predictor. exp(Estimate) is the odds ratio


Std. Error
How uncertain the estimate is


z value
Estimate / Std. Error


Pr(>|z|)
The chance of a z this large if the true effect were 0




Null deviance and Residual deviance measure how badly the model without and with the predictors fits (lower is better). Their difference is the likelihood-ratio test of all the predictors together.
Number of Fisher Scoring iterations is the number of steps R took to find the estimates. Usually 4 to 8. Remember it: a large number is a warning sign in section 5.

Compare with the truth:


Code
data.frame(truth = b_true, estimate = round(coef(fit), 3), se = round(sqrt(diag(vcov(fit))), 3),
           odds_ratio_true = round(exp(b_true), 2), odds_ratio_estimated = round(exp(coef(fit)), 2))


            truth estimate    se odds_ratio_true odds_ratio_estimated
(Intercept) -3.61   -3.707 0.053            0.03                 0.02
marker       1.00    1.046 0.038            2.72                 2.85
age10        0.50    0.493 0.036            1.65                 1.64
smoker       1.00    1.073 0.088            2.72                 2.92


Every estimate is within about two standard errors of the truth. The 95/5 split did not bias anything.
There is one more check, and it holds exactly. Logistic regression with an intercept makes the average predicted probability equal to the share of 1s in the data:


Code
p_train <- predict(fit, type = "response")   # type = "response": probabilities, not log-odds
c(average_predicted = mean(p_train), share_sick = mean(train$disease))


average_predicted        share_sick 
          0.04775           0.04775 


Why exactly? The intercept’s estimating equation is \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) = 0\). So the model knows that the disease is rare, and its probabilities are honest about it.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
text:
3. Problem 1: the 0.5 cutoff
Now we use the model to classify: call a person sick if their predicted probability is above 0.5, the default of many tools.


Code
p_test <- predict(fit, newdata = test, type = "response")
called_sick <- p_test > 0.5
table(truth = test$disease, called_sick)


     called_sick
truth FALSE  TRUE
    0 94766    75
    1  5048   111




Code
c(accuracy             = mean(called_sick == (test$disease == 1)),
  accuracy_call_nobody = mean(test$disease == 0),         # call everybody healthy
  sick_people_caught   = mean(called_sick[test$disease == 1]))


            accuracy accuracy_call_nobody   sick_people_caught 
           0.9487700            0.9484100            0.0215158 


The model is 94.9% accurate, no better than calling everybody healthy, and it catches only 2.2% of the sick people. It looks like a useless model. It is not: the cutoff is the problem.

Why almost nobody passes 0.5
Take a person at the very top of the risk scale: a 60-year-old smoker with a marker 2 SD above average.


Code
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(marker = 2, age10 = 1, smoker = 1), type = "response")


        1 
0.4879954 


This person’s risk is about 10 times the average, and still below 0.5. When the base rate is 5%, a probability of 0.2 or 0.3 already means very high risk. The plot shows the predicted probabilities of the healthy and the sick people of the test set, drawn with plot_separability() of the rwf package:


Code
plot_separability(observed = test$disease, predicted = p_test) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.51, y = Inf, label = "0.5 cutoff", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0" = "#0082c8", "1" = "#E74C3C"), labels = c("healthy (0)", "sick (1)")) +
  labs(title = "Predicted probabilities of the healthy and the sick", x = "predicted probability of disease",
       y = "density", colour = NULL, caption = NULL)









The sick people (red) do get higher probabilities than the healthy ones (blue). The model does tell them apart. But nearly all of both curves lies left of 0.5, so a 0.5 cutoff throws that information away.


Choosing the cutoff from the costs of the two errors
A classification can go wrong in two ways:

False negative (FN): a sick person called healthy. Cost \(C_{FN}\).
False positive (FP): a healthy person called sick. Cost \(C_{FP}\).

For a person with probability \(p\) of being sick:

calling them healthy costs \(C_{FN}\) with probability \(p\), so on average \(p \cdot C_{FN}\);
calling them sick costs \(C_{FP}\) with probability \(1 - p\), so on average \((1 - p) \cdot C_{FP}\).

Call them sick when that is cheaper: \((1 - p)\,C_{FP} < p\,C_{FN}\), which gives
\[\text{call sick when}\quad p > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}}\]
If both errors cost the same, the cutoff is 0.5. If missing a sick person is 10 times worse than a false alarm (say, a false alarm means one more test, while a missed case goes untreated), the cutoff is \(1 / (1 + 10) = 0.091\).
The formula needs honest probabilities: a \(p\) of 0.1 must really mean 10%. We saw in section 2 that logistic regression gives them. Keep this in mind for section 6.


Code
# what a cutoff does: everything is a share of the test set, or of a group of it
metrics <- function(y, p, cut) {
  flag <- p > cut                                    # called sick
  c(cutoff      = cut,
    called_sick = mean(flag),                        # share of all people called sick
    sensitivity = mean(flag[y == 1]),                # sick people caught (recall)
    specificity = mean(!flag[y == 0]),               # healthy people cleared
    precision   = mean(y[flag]),                     # called sick who really are sick (PPV)
    accuracy    = mean(flag == (y == 1)))
}
cost_fn <- 10; cost_fp <- 1
cut_cost <- cost_fp / (cost_fp + cost_fn)
prevalence <- mean(train$disease)

cuts <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, cut_cost, prevalence)
tab <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(cuts, function(k) metrics(test$disease, p_test, k))))
# expected cost per 1,000 people: 10 per missed case, 1 per false alarm
tab$cost_per_1000 <- sapply(cuts, function(k) {
  flag <- p_test > k
  1000 * (cost_fn * mean(test$disease == 1 & !flag) + cost_fp * mean(test$disease == 0 & flag))
})
round(tab, 3)


  cutoff called_sick sensitivity specificity precision accuracy cost_per_1000
1  0.500       0.002       0.022       0.999     0.597    0.949        505.55
2  0.300       0.012       0.093       0.992     0.390    0.946        475.59
3  0.200       0.035       0.202       0.974     0.299    0.934        436.24
4  0.091       0.140       0.475       0.878     0.175    0.857        386.17
5  0.048       0.305       0.703       0.716     0.119    0.716        422.02



At 0.5, almost nobody is called sick: high accuracy, but nearly every sick person is missed, and the cost is the highest.
At 0.091 (the cost cutoff), about 48% of the sick are caught, while 14% of all people are called sick. Accuracy drops, yet this cutoff has the lowest cost: accuracy counts both errors as equally bad, which is exactly what we said they are not.
Precision is modest at every cutoff that catches a useful share of the sick: at the cost cutoff, about 1 in 6 people called sick really is sick. With 95 healthy people for every 5 sick ones, even a small share of false alarms among the healthy outnumbers the true alarms. That is a fact about rare outcomes, not a fault of the model.

The cost curve finds nearly the same cutoff as the formula (the small difference is noise in the test set):


Code
grid <- seq(0.01, 0.6, by = 0.005)
curve_df <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(grid, function(k) metrics(test$disease, p_test, k))))
curve_df$cost <- sapply(grid, function(k) {
  flag <- p_test > k
  1000 * (cost_fn * mean(test$disease == 1 & !flag) + cost_fp * mean(test$disease == 0 & flag))
})
long <- rbind(data.frame(cutoff = grid, value = curve_df$sensitivity, measure = "sensitivity"),
              data.frame(cutoff = grid, value = curve_df$specificity, measure = "specificity"),
              data.frame(cutoff = grid, value = curve_df$precision,   measure = "precision"))
p1 <- ggplot(long, aes(cutoff, value, colour = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(cut_cost, 0.5), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(sensitivity = "#E74C3C", specificity = "#0082c8", precision = "#f39c12")) +
  labs(title = "What each cutoff catches", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)
p2 <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(cutoff, cost)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(cut_cost, 0.5), linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = cut_cost + 0.01, y = max(curve_df$cost), label = "cost cutoff", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.49, y = max(curve_df$cost), label = "0.5", hjust = 1, size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Cost per 1,000 people (a missed case costs 10, a false alarm 1)",
       x = "cutoff", y = "cost")
p1 / p2









Code
c(formula = cut_cost, lowest_cost_on_the_curve = grid[which.min(curve_df$cost)])


                 formula lowest_cost_on_the_curve 
              0.09090909               0.08500000 




When nobody can name the costs
A common choice is the cutoff that maximises sensitivity + specificity (Youden’s index):


Code
roc_test <- roc(test$disease, p_test, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
coords(roc_test, "best", best.method = "youden", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"))


   threshold sensitivity specificity
1 0.04229693    0.743555   0.6784513


For a model with honest probabilities this cutoff lands near the base rate (here 0.048). That is no accident: maximising sensitivity + specificity is the cost rule with \(C_{FN} / C_{FP} = (1 - \pi) / \pi\), where \(\pi\) is the base rate, and then the formula gives \(p > \pi\). So at a 5% base rate, Youden’s cutoff quietly assumes that missing one sick person is as bad as 20 false alarms. Be aware of that choice.


Sometimes you need no cutoff at all
If the decision is “whom do we test first”, rank the people by \(p\) and work down the list as far as resources allow. If the decision is made by a doctor or a manager, give them the probability itself. A cutoff is only needed when a yes/no answer must come out of the model.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
section: 4. Problem 2: judging the model by accuracy
text:
4. Problem 2: judging the model by accuracy
Accuracy rewards the model for the easy part, the healthy majority. Better measures look at each group separately, or at the probabilities themselves.

Discrimination: the AUC
The AUC (area under the ROC curve) is the chance that a randomly chosen sick person gets a higher predicted probability than a randomly chosen healthy person. 0.5 is a coin toss and 1 is perfect. It compares the sick with the healthy within their own groups, so the base rate does not change it.


Code
auc(roc_test)


Area under the curve: 0.7837


Code
ci.auc(roc_test)    # 95% confidence interval (DeLong)


95% CI: 0.7774-0.79 (DeLong)


Code
# the same thing by brute force: draw random sick-healthy pairs, and count how often the sick person is ranked higher
set.seed(1)
sick_p    <- sample(p_test[test$disease == 1], 1e5, replace = TRUE)
healthy_p <- sample(p_test[test$disease == 0], 1e5, replace = TRUE)
mean(sick_p > healthy_p)


[1] 0.78556


What is the best AUC possible with these three predictors? The true model:


Code
p_true <- plogis(b_true[1] + b_true[2] * test$marker + b_true[3] * test$age10 + b_true[4] * test$smoker)
auc(roc(test$disease, p_true, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))


Area under the curve: 0.7838


Our model is as good as the truth. The poor sensitivity at 0.5 was never a fault of the model.


The ROC and precision-recall curves


Code
th <- quantile(p_test, seq(0, 0.999, length.out = 400))
rc <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(th, function(k) metrics(test$disease, p_test, k))))
marks <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(c(0.5, cut_cost, prevalence), function(k) metrics(test$disease, p_test, k))))
marks$label <- c("0.5", "cost cutoff", "base rate")

p_roc <- ggplot(rc, aes(1 - specificity, sensitivity)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = marks, colour = "#E74C3C", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(label = label), hjust = -0.15, vjust = 1.2, size = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "ROC curve", x = "false alarm rate (1 - specificity)", y = "sensitivity")
p_pr <- ggplot(rc, aes(sensitivity, precision)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = prevalence, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = marks, colour = "#E74C3C", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(label = label), hjust = -0.15, vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Precision-recall curve", x = "sensitivity (recall)", y = "precision")
p_roc + p_pr










The ROC curve (left) does not depend on the base rate. The dotted diagonal is a coin toss.
The precision-recall curve (right) does. Its dotted baseline is the base rate, 0.048: the precision of calling people sick at random. Use it when what matters is how many of the people you flag really are sick. It is honest about how hard a rare outcome is.



Are the probabilities right? Brier score and calibration
The Brier score is the mean squared difference between the predicted probability and what happened (0 or 1). Lower is better. A model that gives everybody the base rate scores \(\pi(1 - \pi)\), so the scaled Brier score \(1 - \text{Brier} / [\pi(1 - \pi)]\) is the improvement over knowing nothing but the base rate.


Code
brier <- function(y, p) mean((p - y)^2)
base_rate_test <- mean(test$disease)                 # the base rate of the people we judge the model on
b_model <- brier(test$disease, p_test)
b_null  <- base_rate_test * (1 - base_rate_test)     # give everybody the base rate
c(brier = b_model, brier_base_rate_only = b_null, scaled_brier = 1 - b_model / b_null)


               brier brier_base_rate_only         scaled_brier 
          0.04486773           0.04892847           0.08299347 


The model improves on the base rate by about 8%. That sounds small, but it is typical: with a rare outcome both numbers are small and close together, because predicting “almost 0” for everybody is already nearly right. Use the Brier score to compare models fitted to the same outcome, not on its own.
Calibration asks whether a predicted 10% really comes true 10% of the time. Sort the people into 20 groups by predicted probability and compare each group’s average prediction with the share who are sick:


Code
calibration_bins <- function(y, p, bins = 20) {
  g <- cut(p, unique(quantile(p, seq(0, 1, length.out = bins + 1))), include.lowest = TRUE)
  data.frame(predicted = as.numeric(tapply(p, g, mean)), observed = as.numeric(tapply(y, g, mean)))
}
cal <- calibration_bins(test$disease, p_test)
ggplot(cal, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", size = 2.5) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, max(cal)), ylim = c(0, max(cal))) +
  labs(title = "Calibration: predicted risk against the share who are sick",
       x = "average predicted probability (20 groups)", y = "share sick in the group")









The points lie close to the diagonal. They sit slightly above it because, by chance, the training sample has a few fewer sick people (4.8%) than the test set (5.2%). Two numbers summarise the plot:


Code
lp <- qlogis(p_test)                                                         # predictions as log-odds
c(calibration_intercept = unname(coef(glm(test$disease ~ offset(lp), family = binomial))[1]),   # ideal 0
  calibration_slope     = unname(coef(glm(test$disease ~ lp, family = binomial))[2]))           # ideal 1


calibration_intercept     calibration_slope 
           0.07899984            0.95165337 



Calibration intercept (ideal 0): are the predictions too high (negative) or too low (positive) on average?
Calibration slope (ideal 1): below 1, the predictions are too extreme, the typical sign of an overfitted model; above 1, too timid.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
text:
5. Problem 3: too few events
So far we had 955 sick people. Now the problem that is real: a small sample, where 5% is only a handful of people.

A small sample: separation


Code
set.seed(46)
small <- simulate_people(200)
c(people = nrow(small), sick = sum(small$disease))


people   sick 
   200     10 


Code
table(smoker = small$smoker, disease = small$disease)


      disease
smoker   0   1
     0 172  10
     1  18   0


Only 10 people are sick, and by chance none of the 18 smokers is. Ordinary logistic regression:


Code
fit_small <- glm(disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, family = binomial, data = small)
summary(fit_small)



Call:
glm(formula = disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, family = binomial, 
    data = small)

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)   -3.24939    0.43961  -7.392 1.45e-13 ***
marker         0.79318    0.32754   2.422   0.0155 *  
age10          0.07154    0.33284   0.215   0.8298    
smoker       -15.17658 1493.28802  -0.010   0.9919    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 79.406  on 199  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 70.988  on 196  degrees of freedom
AIC: 78.988

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 17


Look at smoker: an estimate of about -15, an odds ratio of 0.0000003, which says that smokers cannot get the disease, with an enormous standard error. In truth smoking multiplies the odds by 2.7.
This is separation. Because no smoker is sick, the likelihood keeps increasing as the smoker coefficient goes towards \(-\infty\), so the best estimate does not exist. R stops when the improvement becomes tiny, after 17 iterations instead of the usual 4 to 8, and reports wherever it stopped. Sometimes glm() warns “fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred”, often, as here, it says nothing. Signs to look for: a huge estimate, a huge standard error, many iterations, and a category of a predictor with no 1s (or no 0s) in it.


The fix: Firth’s penalised likelihood
Ordinary logistic regression maximises the log-likelihood \(\log L(\beta)\). Firth’s method maximises a penalised version:
\[\log L^*(\beta) = \log L(\beta) + \tfrac{1}{2} \log \left| I(\beta) \right|\]
\(I(\beta)\) is the Fisher information: how much the data can tell us about \(\beta\). It is largest when the predicted probabilities are away from 0 and 1, and it shrinks towards 0 as a coefficient runs off to infinity. So the penalty pulls the estimates back from infinity, by a lot when the data say little (as for the smokers here) and by almost nothing when the data say much. It also removes most of the small-sample bias of ordinary maximum likelihood, which makes coefficients too large in small samples. In R, logistf() fits it (install.packages("logistf")):


Code
fit_firth <- logistf(disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, data = small)
summary(fit_firth)


logistf(formula = disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, data = small)

Model fitted by Penalized ML
Coefficients:
                   coef  se(coef) lower 0.95 upper 0.95      Chisq          p method
(Intercept) -3.08649293 0.4004973 -4.0331079  -2.382327        Inf 0.00000000      2
marker       0.74629289 0.2987553  0.1483080   1.402900 6.04305392 0.01396111      2
age10        0.08679259 0.3021880 -0.5682952   0.712907 0.07135286 0.78937710      2
smoker      -0.37756420 1.4498505 -5.2664768   1.846124 0.07075176 0.79024535      2

Method: 1-Wald, 2-Profile penalized log-likelihood, 3-None

Likelihood ratio test=6.532561 on 3 df, p=0.0883872, n=200
Wald test = 74.32831 on 3 df, p = 5.551115e-16



coef are the estimates. The smoker effect is now finite.
lower 0.95, upper 0.95 are 95% confidence intervals from the profile penalised likelihood. They are better than estimate ± 1.96 SE in small samples, because they need not be symmetric.
Chisq and p test each coefficient against 0 with a likelihood-ratio test.

The smoker interval is very wide, and it should be: 18 smokers and no case among them tell us very little. Firth gives an honest “we do not know much” instead of a nonsense “never”.


Code
round(data.frame(truth = b_true, glm = coef(fit_small), firth = coef(fit_firth)), 2)


            truth    glm firth
(Intercept) -3.61  -3.25 -3.09
marker       1.00   0.79  0.75
age10        0.50   0.07  0.09
smoker       1.00 -15.18 -0.38




Firth’s predictions: correct the intercept with flic()
The Firth penalty also pulls the intercept towards 0, which pushes the predicted probabilities towards 0.5. With a rare outcome they come out a little too high on average. flic() (Firth’s logistic regression with intercept correction) keeps Firth’s slopes and re-estimates the intercept, so that the average prediction again equals the share of 1s:


Code
fit_flic <- flic(fit_firth)
c(share_sick    = mean(small$disease),
  glm           = mean(predict(fit_small, type = "response")),
  firth         = mean(predict(fit_firth, newdata = small, type = "response")),
  firth_flic    = mean(predict(fit_flic,  newdata = small, type = "response")))


share_sick        glm      firth firth_flic 
0.05000000 0.05000000 0.05833987 0.05000000 


Use logistf() for the coefficients (odds ratios and their intervals) and flic() for predicted probabilities.


How many events are enough? A simulation
One sample proves little. We draw 500 samples at each of five sizes, always with a 5% base rate, fit ordinary and Firth logistic regression to each, and compare the estimates with the truth.


Code
one_sample <- function(n) {
  d <- simulate_people(n)
  g <- suppressWarnings(glm(disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, family = binomial, data = d))
  f <- logistf(disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, data = d, pl = FALSE)   # pl = FALSE: skip the intervals, faster
  c(n = n, events = sum(d$disease),
    separation = sum(d$disease[d$smoker == 1]) == 0,                     # no sick smoker in the sample
    glm_marker = unname(coef(g)["marker"]), firth_marker = unname(coef(f)["marker"]),
    glm_smoker = unname(coef(g)["smoker"]), firth_smoker = unname(coef(f)["smoker"]))
}
sizes <- c(200, 400, 1000, 2000, 5000)
set.seed(1)
sim <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, lapply(sizes, function(n) t(replicate(500, one_sample(n))))))

rmse <- function(x, truth) sqrt(mean((x - truth)^2))   # typical distance from the truth
sim_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(sim, sim$n), function(s) data.frame(
  n                  = s$n[1],
  events             = round(mean(s$events)),
  separation_pct     = round(100 * mean(s$separation), 1),
  marker_glm_mean    = round(mean(s$glm_marker), 3),
  marker_firth_mean  = round(mean(s$firth_marker), 3),
  marker_glm_sd      = round(sd(s$glm_marker), 3),
  smoker_glm_rmse    = round(rmse(s$glm_smoker, 1), 2),
  smoker_firth_rmse  = round(rmse(s$firth_smoker, 1), 2))))
sim_table


        n events separation_pct marker_glm_mean marker_firth_mean marker_glm_sd smoker_glm_rmse smoker_firth_rmse
200   200     10           13.8           1.109             1.015         0.473            6.27              0.86
400   400     20            3.0           1.041             1.003         0.292            2.98              0.69
1000 1000     50            0.0           1.000             0.986         0.175            0.39              0.37
2000 2000    100            0.0           1.013             1.006         0.122            0.29              0.28
5000 5000    251            0.0           1.002             0.999         0.072            0.18              0.17




Code
sim$size <- factor(paste0(sim$n, " people\n~", round(ave(sim$events, sim$n)), " events"),
                   levels = unique(paste0(sim$n, " people\n~", round(ave(sim$events, sim$n)), " events")))
long_sim <- rbind(
  data.frame(size = sim$size, coefficient = "marker (truth 1)", method = "glm",   estimate = sim$glm_marker),
  data.frame(size = sim$size, coefficient = "marker (truth 1)", method = "Firth", estimate = sim$firth_marker),
  data.frame(size = sim$size, coefficient = "smoker (truth 1)", method = "glm",   estimate = sim$glm_smoker),
  data.frame(size = sim$size, coefficient = "smoker (truth 1)", method = "Firth", estimate = sim$firth_smoker))
ggplot(long_sim, aes(size, estimate, fill = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~coefficient, ncol = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-2.5, 4)) +   # glm's separated estimates (around -16) are below the chart
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(glm = "#E74C3C", Firth = "#0082c8")) +
  labs(title = "Estimates from 500 samples of each size, all with a 5% base rate",
       x = NULL, y = "estimated coefficient", fill = NULL)









What the table and plot show:

The base rate is 5% in every row. The precision is not. The spread of the marker estimate (marker_glm_sd) falls from 0.473 with about 10 events to 0.072 with about 251: roughly in proportion to \(1/\sqrt{\text{events}}\). What matters is how many 1s there are, not what percentage they are.
With about 10 events, 13.8% of the samples had no sick smoker, and in those glm() gave a smoker coefficient around -16 (below the chart). Its typical error for smokers (smoker_glm_rmse) is 6.27, against 0.86 for Firth. Even for the marker, glm() overestimates the effect on average (1.109 instead of 1), while Firth is close to 1.
From about 100 events on, the two methods agree and both are right. Firth costs nothing when there is enough data, so it is a safe default when events are few.



Rules of thumb for the number of events

The classic rule is at least 10 events per estimated coefficient (Peduzzi et al., 1996). Count every coefficient: each dummy of a categorical predictor, each interaction, and every predictor you tried, not only the ones you kept.
“Events” means the rarer class. If 95% were 1s, count the 0s.
The rule is rough. Modern guidance (Riley et al., 2020; van Smeden et al., 2016) computes the sample size a model needs from the base rate, the number of predictors and the expected fit. The pmsampsize package does the calculation.
With few events and many predictors, use fewer predictors, or a penalised regression (ridge, lasso, elastic net) that shrinks all coefficients. The Regularized Regression tutorial shows how; glmnet(..., family = "binomial") does it for a binary outcome.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
section: 6. Problem 4: the popular “fixes” make it worse
text:
6. Problem 4: the popular “fixes” make it worse
The usual advice for imbalance is to balance the data before fitting:

Undersampling: keep all the 1s and only as many randomly chosen 0s.
Oversampling: keep all the 0s and copy randomly chosen 1s until there are as many.
Class weights: give each 1 a weight of \(n_0 / n_1\) (here about 20), so the two classes weigh the same.
SMOTE: like oversampling, but it makes up new 1s between existing ones. It has the same problem as the others (van den Goorbergh et al., 2022), so we do not run it here.



Code
set.seed(7)
ones  <- train[train$disease == 1, ]
zeros <- train[train$disease == 0, ]
n1 <- nrow(ones); n0 <- nrow(zeros)
under <- rbind(ones, zeros[sample(n0, n1), ])                    # all 1s, as many random 0s
over  <- rbind(zeros, ones[sample(n1, n0, replace = TRUE), ])    # all 0s, 1s copied up to as many
w     <- ifelse(train$disease == 1, round(n0 / n1), 1)           # weight about 20 for each 1

form <- disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker
models <- list("original"      = fit,
               "undersampled"  = glm(form, family = binomial, data = under),
               "oversampled"   = glm(form, family = binomial, data = over),
               "class weights" = glm(form, family = binomial, data = train, weights = w))

summarise_model <- function(m) {
  p <- predict(m, newdata = test, type = "response")
  c(rows_used          = nrow(m$model),
    intercept          = unname(coef(m)[1]),
    marker             = unname(coef(m)["marker"]),
    marker_se          = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))["marker"]),
    average_prediction = mean(p),
    auc                = as.numeric(auc(roc(test$disease, p, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))),
    brier              = brier(test$disease, p))
}
round(t(sapply(models, summarise_model)), 3)


              rows_used intercept marker marker_se average_prediction   auc brier
original          20000    -3.707  1.046     0.038              0.048 0.784 0.045
undersampled       1910    -0.744  1.059     0.061              0.380 0.784 0.185
oversampled       38090    -0.734  1.089     0.014              0.381 0.784 0.187
class weights     20000    -0.735  1.087     0.014              0.382 0.784 0.187


Row by row:

auc is the same for all four. Balancing did not make the model better at telling the sick from the healthy, not even a little.
marker is about the same. The slopes barely move: balancing does not change how risk depends on the predictors.
intercept jumped from about \(-3.7\) to about \(-0.75\). That is \(\log(n_0 / n_1) = \log(19.9) = 2.99\) higher: the balanced models think the base rate is 50%.
average_prediction is therefore about 0.38 instead of 0.048. The probabilities are about 8 times too high on average, and the Brier score is worse. You can no longer read them as risks, or use them with the cost cutoff of section 3.
marker_se is too small for oversampling and weights (0.014 against 0.038): the copies of the same sick people are counted as new people, so confidence intervals and p values are far too optimistic. Undersampling has the opposite problem: it threw away 18,090 people and their information, so its SE is larger.

The calibration plot shows the damage:


Code
cal_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(nm) {
  p <- predict(models[[nm]], newdata = test, type = "response")
  data.frame(calibration_bins(test$disease, p), model = nm)
}))
cal_all$model <- factor(cal_all$model, levels = names(models))
ggplot(cal_all, aes(predicted, observed, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("original" = "black", "undersampled" = "#E74C3C",
                                 "oversampled" = "#f39c12", "class weights" = "#8E44AD")) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Balanced models predict far more disease than there is",
       x = "average predicted probability (20 groups)", y = "share sick in the group", colour = NULL)









The original model sits on the diagonal (in the bottom-left corner, where the risks of a rare disease are). The three balanced models lie on top of each other, far below it: where they predict about 60%, only about 7% are sick.

All that balancing did was move the cutoff
Why does balancing seem to “work” for people who use the 0.5 cutoff? Undersampling the 0s by a factor \(r\) multiplies the odds by \(r\), so it adds \(\log r\) to every log-odds:
\[\text{log-odds}_{\text{balanced}} \approx \text{log-odds}_{\text{original}} + \log\frac{1 - \pi}{\pi}\]
So \(p_{\text{balanced}} > 0.5\) (log-odds above 0) is the same as \(\text{log-odds}_{\text{original}} > \log\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}\), which is \(p_{\text{original}} > \pi\). The balanced model at 0.5 classifies like the original model at the base rate:


Code
p_under <- predict(models[["undersampled"]], newdata = test, type = "response")
agree <- table(original_at_base_rate = p_test > prevalence, balanced_at_0.5 = p_under > 0.5)
agree


                     balanced_at_0.5
original_at_base_rate FALSE  TRUE
                FALSE 69280   200
                TRUE    596 29924


Code
c(agreement = sum(diag(agree)) / sum(agree))


agreement 
  0.99204 


The two classify 99.2% of people the same way. The small differences come from the random 0s that undersampling kept. Balancing is a roundabout way of choosing a cutoff, and it costs you honest probabilities, correct standard errors or data. Moving the cutoff of the original model (section 3) gets the same classifications with none of these costs.


If you did sample on the outcome: correct the intercept
Sometimes sampling on the outcome is a good design. If measuring the predictors is expensive (a lab test, an interview), it is sensible to measure all the sick people and only some of the healthy ones: a case-control design. The slopes from such a sample are still valid (Prentice & Pyke, 1979). Only the intercept is off, and it can be corrected if the true base rate \(\tau\) is known (King & Zeng, 2001):
\[\hat\beta_0^{\text{corrected}} = \hat\beta_0 - \log\left[\frac{\bar y}{1 - \bar y} \cdot \frac{1 - \tau}{\tau}\right]\]
where \(\bar y\) is the share of 1s in the sample (0.5 here) and \(\tau\) the share in the population.


Code
m_under <- models[["undersampled"]]
y_bar   <- mean(under$disease)          # 0.5 in the balanced sample
tau     <- prevalence                   # the true base rate, known from elsewhere
m_corrected <- m_under
m_corrected$coefficients[1] <- coef(m_under)[1] - log((y_bar / (1 - y_bar)) * ((1 - tau) / tau))

p_corrected <- predict(m_corrected, newdata = test, type = "response")
round(c(intercept_truth = unname(b_true[1]), intercept_original = unname(coef(fit)[1]),
        intercept_corrected = unname(coef(m_corrected)[1]),
        average_prediction_original = mean(p_test), average_prediction_corrected = mean(p_corrected)), 3)


             intercept_truth           intercept_original          intercept_corrected  average_prediction_original average_prediction_corrected 
                      -3.610                       -3.707                       -3.737                        0.048                        0.048 


After the correction the undersampled model predicts like the model fitted to all the data, from 1,910 people instead of 20,000. Its standard errors are larger, the price of the smaller sample, but they are correct.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
section: 7. A workflow for a rare outcome
text:
7. A workflow for a rare outcome
In practice there is no test set of 100,000. Judge the model on data it has not seen: hold out part of the data, or use cross-validation or the bootstrap. The steps:

Count the events (the rarer class) and the coefficients. Below about 10 events per coefficient, or with separation, use Firth (logistf(), and flic() for predictions), fewer predictors, or a penalised regression.
Fit on the data as they are. Do not balance them.
Judge the model with the AUC (and, if you care about the flagged people, the precision-recall curve), the Brier score and a calibration plot, never with accuracy alone.
Choose a cutoff from the costs of the two errors, \(p > C_{FP} / (C_{FP} + C_{FN})\), or give the probabilities themselves.
Report the number of events, the model and how you judged it (section 8).

Here are the steps with 10-fold cross-validation on the training data. Every person gets a prediction from a model fitted without them:


Code
set.seed(11)
k <- 10
fold <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(train)))
p_cv <- numeric(nrow(train))
for (i in 1:k) {
  m <- glm(disease ~ marker + age10 + smoker, family = binomial, data = train[fold != i, ])
  p_cv[fold == i] <- predict(m, newdata = train[fold == i, ], type = "response")
}
c(events                 = sum(train$disease),
  events_per_coefficient = sum(train$disease) / 3,
  auc_cv                 = as.numeric(auc(roc(train$disease, p_cv, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))),
  scaled_brier_cv        = 1 - brier(train$disease, p_cv) / (prevalence * (1 - prevalence)),
  calibration_slope_cv   = unname(coef(glm(train$disease ~ qlogis(p_cv), family = binomial))[2]))


                events events_per_coefficient                 auc_cv        scaled_brier_cv   calibration_slope_cv 
          955.00000000           318.33333333             0.79712948             0.08174037             0.99638144 


Code
round(metrics(train$disease, p_cv, cut_cost), 3)


     cutoff called_sick sensitivity specificity   precision    accuracy 
      0.091       0.138       0.489       0.879       0.169       0.861 


The cross-validated numbers are close to what the test set of 100,000 showed, so in real data, where there is no such test set, cross-validation tells the same story.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) should give the number of events, the effects with their uncertainty, and how well the model predicts: discrimination, calibration and, if you classify, the cutoff and why. We collect the numbers from the R objects:


Code
or    <- exp(coef(fit))
or_ci <- exp(confint(fit))                                      # profile-likelihood 95% CI
s     <- summary(fit)$coefficients
auc_ci <- as.numeric(ci.auc(roc_test))                          # lower, AUC, upper
cal_slope <- unname(coef(glm(test$disease ~ qlogis(p_test), family = binomial))[2])
at_cut <- metrics(test$disease, p_test, cut_cost)

f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))


Method (data analysis):

Disease status was analysed with logistic regression, with the blood marker, age (in decades) and smoking as predictors. Of the 20,000 participants, 955 (4.8%) had the disease, giving 318 events per estimated coefficient. The data were not resampled or weighted. Predictive performance was assessed in an independent validation sample (N = 100,000) with the area under the ROC curve (AUC), the Brier score and the calibration slope. Participants were classified as at risk when their predicted probability exceeded .091, the cutoff that minimises the expected cost when a missed case is judged 10 times as costly as a false alarm. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the pROC package.

Results:

A higher marker level, OR = 2.85, 95% CI [2.65, 3.07], p < .001, older age, OR = 1.64 per decade, 95% CI [1.53, 1.76], p < .001, and smoking, OR = 2.92, 95% CI [2.45, 3.47], p < .001, were each associated with higher odds of disease. In the validation sample the model discriminated well, AUC = .78, 95% CI [.78, .79], and was well calibrated (calibration slope = 0.95; Brier score = .045, against .049 for predicting the base rate). At the cutoff of .091, sensitivity was .48, specificity .88 and the positive predictive value .18, with 14.0% of participants classified as at risk.

Points to remember:

Give the number of events, not only the percentage, and say that the data were not resampled. If they were sampled on the outcome (case-control), say how the intercept was corrected.
Report discrimination (AUC) and calibration (calibration plot or slope, Brier score), not accuracy alone.
If you classify, give the cutoff and the reason for it, with sensitivity, specificity and the positive predictive value at that cutoff.
With few events or separation, say that you used Firth’s penalised likelihood, and give its profile-likelihood intervals.
Cite R and the packages; citation(), citation("pROC") and citation("logistf") in R give the exact references.

title: Logistic Regression With a Rare Outcome: Is a 95/5 Split a Problem?
text:
9. Summary







Is 95/5 a problem?
Not by itself. Logistic regression estimates the slopes without bias and gives honest probabilities whatever the split


The 0.5 cutoff
With a rare outcome almost nobody passes it. Use \(p > C_{FP} / (C_{FP} + C_{FN})\), or give the probabilities


Accuracy
Calling everybody 0 is already 95% accurate. Use the AUC, the precision-recall curve, the Brier score and a calibration plot


Few events
The real problem: count the 1s, not the percentage. Aim for 10 or more events per coefficient


Separation
A huge estimate and SE, many iterations, a category with no 1s. Use Firth: logistf(), with flic() for predictions


Under/oversampling, SMOTE, weights
Same AUC, wrong probabilities, wrong (or wasted) standard errors. They only move the cutoff


Case-control data
Slopes are fine. Correct the intercept with the known base rate


R
glm(y ~ x, family = binomial); logistf::logistf() and flic(); pROC::roc(), auc(), ci.auc(), coords()

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
text:
At the end of every term, students at the University of Texas at Austin rated their courses from 1 (very unsatisfactory) to 5 (excellent). For 463 courses taught between 2000 and 2002, economists Daniel Hamermesh and Amy Parker also asked six students to rate the physical appearance of each instructor from their photograph. Their question: do better-looking instructors get better evaluations (Hamermesh & Parker, 2005)?
A simple correlation is not enough to answer it. Beauty might go together with other things that also affect evaluations: age, gender, the kind of course, the size of the class. The real question is one of incremental validity:

Does beauty predict teaching evaluations over and above who the instructor is and what they teach?

Hierarchical regression answers exactly this kind of question. We enter the predictors in blocks, in an order decided in advance, and after each block we ask how much more of the variance of the outcome the model explains. That increase is the R² change, \(\Delta R^2\), and the F-change test tells us whether it is larger than chance.
The predictor of interest goes in last, so it gets credit only for what the earlier blocks cannot explain. If beauty still adds something after everything else, that is strong evidence that it matters on its own.
A note on the name. “Hierarchical” here means the order in which blocks of predictors enter the model. It has nothing to do with hierarchical linear models, also called multilevel or mixed models, which are for data nested in groups (students in schools, courses in instructors). Those have their own tutorial: Multilevel Models. We will meet the nesting issue in section 8, because these data have it too.


Code
library(AER)        # the data: TeachingRatings
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots together
library(car)        # vif(): checks multicollinearity
library(sandwich)   # vcovCL(): cluster-robust standard errors (section 8)
library(lmtest)     # coeftest() and waldtest() with those standard errors
library(ggfortify)  # needed by rwf's report_regression() for its diagnostic plots (section 7)

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
text:
At the end of every term, students at the University of Texas at Austin rated their courses from 1 (very unsatisfactory) to 5 (excellent). For 463 courses taught between 2000 and 2002, economists Daniel Hamermesh and Amy Parker also asked six students to rate the physical appearance of each instructor from their photograph. Their question: do better-looking instructors get better evaluations (Hamermesh & Parker, 2005)?
A simple correlation is not enough to answer it. Beauty might go together with other things that also affect evaluations: age, gender, the kind of course, the size of the class. The real question is one of incremental validity:

Does beauty predict teaching evaluations over and above who the instructor is and what they teach?

Hierarchical regression answers exactly this kind of question. We enter the predictors in blocks, in an order decided in advance, and after each block we ask how much more of the variance of the outcome the model explains. That increase is the R² change, \(\Delta R^2\), and the F-change test tells us whether it is larger than chance.
The predictor of interest goes in last, so it gets credit only for what the earlier blocks cannot explain. If beauty still adds something after everything else, that is strong evidence that it matters on its own.
A note on the name. “Hierarchical” here means the order in which blocks of predictors enter the model. It has nothing to do with hierarchical linear models, also called multilevel or mixed models, which are for data nested in groups (students in schools, courses in instructors). Those have their own tutorial: Multilevel Models. We will meet the nesting issue in section 8, because these data have it too.


Code
library(AER)        # the data: TeachingRatings
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots together
library(car)        # vif(): checks multicollinearity
library(sandwich)   # vcovCL(): cluster-robust standard errors (section 8)
library(lmtest)     # coeftest() and waldtest() with those standard errors
library(ggfortify)  # needed by rwf's report_regression() for its diagnostic plots (section 7)

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
text:
1. The data


Code
data("TeachingRatings", package = "AER")
tr <- TeachingRatings
c(courses = nrow(tr), instructors = length(unique(tr$prof)))


    courses instructors 
        463          94 









Variable
Meaning




eval
The course’s average evaluation, from 1 (very unsatisfactory) to 5 (excellent)


beauty
The instructor’s appearance, rated by six students from a photograph and averaged, shifted to a mean of 0


gender, minority, native, age
The instructor: female or male, from a minority (non-Caucasian) or not, native English speaker or not, age in years


tenure
Is the instructor on the tenure track?


division
An upper-division course, or a lower-division one (mainly large first- and second-year courses)


credits
A single-credit elective (yoga, aerobics, dance) or a regular course


allstudents
The number of students enrolled


prof
Which of the 94 instructors taught the course



We code each yes/no variable as a 0/1 dummy with a clear name, so that every coefficient says what it compares. Age goes in decades, so that its coefficient is not a tiny number per year. Class size is very skewed (8 to 581 students), so we use its base-2 logarithm: one unit more means twice as many students.


Code
d <- data.frame(
  eval           = tr$eval,
  female         = as.integer(tr$gender == "female"),   # 1 = female instructor
  minority       = as.integer(tr$minority == "yes"),    # 1 = minority (non-Caucasian)
  non_native     = as.integer(tr$native == "no"),       # 1 = not a native English speaker
  age            = tr$age / 10,                         # in decades: +1 = ten years older
  tenure_track   = as.integer(tr$tenure == "yes"),      # 1 = on the tenure track
  lower_division = as.integer(tr$division == "lower"),  # 1 = lower-division course
  single_credit  = as.integer(tr$credits == "single"),  # 1 = single-credit elective
  log2_size      = log2(tr$allstudents),                # +1 = class twice as large
  beauty         = tr$beauty,
  prof           = tr$prof)

round(sapply(d[, 1:10], function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), min = min(x), max = max(x))), 2)


     eval female minority non_native  age tenure_track lower_division single_credit log2_size beauty
mean 4.00   0.42     0.14       0.06 4.84         0.78           0.34          0.06      5.15   0.00
sd   0.55   0.49     0.35       0.24 0.98         0.41           0.47          0.23      1.22   0.79
min  2.10   0.00     0.00       0.00 2.90         0.00           0.00          0.00      3.00  -1.45
max  5.00   1.00     1.00       1.00 7.30         1.00           1.00          1.00      9.18   1.97


For the dummies, the mean is the share of courses with a 1: for example, 42% of the courses were taught by women and 6% were single-credit electives. The average evaluation is 4.00 (SD = 0.55): students were generally satisfied.
Hierarchical regression compares models fitted to the same people. If some variables had missing values, each model would drop different rows and the R² values would not be comparable. These data have none, but in your own data remove incomplete rows first, e.g. d <- na.omit(d[, variables_of_all_blocks]).

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
text:
2. Look at the data


Code
r_beauty <- cor(d$beauty, d$eval)
p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(beauty, eval)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#E74C3C", fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.15) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Better-looking instructors get somewhat better evaluations (r = %.2f)", r_beauty),
       x = "beauty rating (0 = average)", y = "course evaluation (1 to 5)")

predictors <- c("female", "minority", "non_native", "age", "tenure_track",
                "lower_division", "single_credit", "log2_size", "beauty")
cors <- data.frame(predictor = factor(predictors, levels = rev(predictors)),
                   with_eval = sapply(d[predictors], cor, y = d$eval))
p2 <- ggplot(cors, aes(with_eval, predictor, fill = with_eval > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#0082c8", `FALSE` = "#E74C3C"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Correlation of each predictor with the evaluation", x = "correlation", y = NULL)
p1 / p2









Beauty correlates 0.19 with the evaluations, so it explains \(r^2\) = 3.6% of their variance on its own. Single-credit electives get the best evaluations; female, non-native and tenure-track instructors, and larger classes, get lower ones. Several of these predictors also correlate with beauty, which is why we need a model that holds them constant.

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
section: 3. The plan: three blocks, chosen in advance
text:
3. The plan: three blocks, chosen in advance









Step
Block
Predictors
Why here




1
Who the instructor is
female, minority, non_native, age
Fixed before any teaching starts, so nothing else can cause them


2
The job and the course
tenure_track, lower_division, single_credit, log2_size
What and whom they teach, and on which contract


3
Appearance
beauty
The predictor of interest: entered last, so it must explain something the first two blocks cannot



The order comes from theory and the research question, decided before looking at the results. Common rules: background variables and things that come first in time go first, control variables go before the predictors of interest, and the predictor whose added value you want to test goes last.
This is the opposite of stepwise regression, where the computer adds or drops predictors according to their p values. Stepwise selection capitalises on chance, and its p values and R² are too optimistic. In hierarchical regression you decide the order, and the data only answer the question you asked.

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
section: 4. Fit the three models and test each step
text:
4. Fit the three models and test each step


Code
m0 <- lm(eval ~ 1, data = d)                                                        # no predictors: R² = 0
m1 <- lm(eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age, data = d)                     # step 1
m2 <- update(m1, . ~ . + tenure_track + lower_division + single_credit + log2_size) # step 2: + block 2
m3 <- update(m2, . ~ . + beauty)                                                    # step 3: + beauty


update(m1, . ~ . + ...) means: the same model as m1, with these predictors added.

The formulas
For a model with \(k\) predictors fitted to \(n\) cases:

R², the share of the variance of the outcome the model explains: \(R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{RSS}{TSS}\), where \(RSS = \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\) is what the model leaves unexplained and \(TSS = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2\) is the total.
Adjusted R² corrects R² for the number of predictors, since adding any predictor, even pure noise, raises R² a little: \(R^2_{adj} = 1 - (1 - R^2)\dfrac{n - 1}{n - k - 1}\)
R² change from a smaller model (1) to a larger one (2): \(\Delta R^2 = R^2_2 - R^2_1\)
F-change, the test of \(\Delta R^2\), where \(\Delta k\) is the number of predictors added and \(k_2\) the number in the larger model:

\[F = \frac{\Delta R^2 / \Delta k}{(1 - R^2_2) / (n - k_2 - 1)}, \qquad \text{with } \Delta k \text{ and } n - k_2 - 1 \text{ degrees of freedom}\]
The top is the variance explained by the new block, per predictor added. The bottom is the variance still unexplained, per remaining degree of freedom. If the new block were useless, the two would be about equal and \(F\) would be close to 1.

Effect size of the change, Cohen’s \(f^2 = \dfrac{\Delta R^2}{1 - R^2_2}\): about .02 is small, .15 medium and .35 large (Cohen, 1988).



The steps by hand


Code
n <- nrow(d)
models <- list(m0, m1, m2, m3)
k_of <- function(m) length(coef(m)) - 1                     # number of predictors
steps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2:4, function(i) {
  small <- models[[i - 1]]; big <- models[[i]]
  r2_small <- summary(small)$r.squared
  r2_big   <- summary(big)$r.squared
  delta    <- r2_big - r2_small
  dk       <- k_of(big) - k_of(small)
  df2      <- n - k_of(big) - 1
  F_change <- (delta / dk) / ((1 - r2_big) / df2)
  data.frame(step = i - 1, k = k_of(big), r2 = r2_big, adj_r2 = summary(big)$adj.r.squared,
             delta_r2 = delta, F_change = F_change, df1 = dk, df2 = df2,
             p = pf(F_change, dk, df2, lower.tail = FALSE), f2 = delta / (1 - r2_big))
}))
steps$block <- c("1: who the instructor is", "2: + the job and the course", "3: + beauty")
format(steps[, c("block", "k", "r2", "adj_r2", "delta_r2", "F_change", "df1", "df2", "p", "f2")], digits = 3)


                        block k     r2 adj_r2 delta_r2 F_change df1 df2        p     f2
1    1: who the instructor is 4 0.0527 0.0444   0.0527     6.37   4 458 5.40e-05 0.0556
2 2: + the job and the course 8 0.1268 0.1114   0.0741     9.63   4 454 1.76e-07 0.0848
3                 3: + beauty 9 0.1726 0.1562   0.0458    25.10   1 453 7.81e-07 0.0554




Code
bars <- data.frame(model = factor(rep(steps$block, 1:3), levels = steps$block),
                   block = factor(c(steps$block[1], steps$block[1:2], steps$block[1:3]), levels = steps$block),
                   value = c(steps$delta_r2[1], steps$delta_r2[1:2], steps$delta_r2[1:3]))
ggplot(bars, aes(model, value, fill = block)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(data = steps, aes(x = block, y = r2, label = sprintf("R² = %.3f\nΔR² = %.3f", r2, delta_r2)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = -0.3, size = 3.2, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#f39c12", "#E74C3C"), labels = c("block 1", "block 2", "beauty")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.22), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Variance of the evaluations explained, step by step", x = NULL, y = "R²", fill = NULL)









Step by step:

Who the instructor is explains 5.3% of the variance of the evaluations, F(4, 458) = 6.37, p < .001.
The job and the course add another 7.4%, F(4, 454) = 9.63, p < .001.
Beauty adds 4.6% more, F(1, 453) = 25.1, p < .001, \(f^2\) = 0.055, a small effect by Cohen’s labels. Beauty predicts evaluations even after all eight other predictors have had their say.

Altogether the model explains 17.3% (adjusted 15.6%). Most of what makes a course well rated is not in these data, which is normal for something as complex as teaching.


The same tests with anova()
R compares nested models with anova(). Comparing each pair gives exactly the F-change of the table above, the value SPSS reports:


Code
anova(m0, m1)


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: eval ~ 1
Model 2: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq     F    Pr(>F)    
1    462 142.24                                 
2    458 134.74  4     7.495 6.369 5.401e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
anova(m1, m2)


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age
Model 2: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track + 
    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F   Pr(>F)    
1    458 134.74                                 
2    454 124.21  4    10.537 9.6287 1.76e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Code
anova(m2, m3)


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track + 
    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size
Model 2: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track + 
    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size + beauty
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    454 124.21                                  
2    453 117.69  1     6.521 25.101 7.813e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


How to read it: Res.Df and RSS are the residual degrees of freedom and the residual sum of squares of each model. Df is the number of predictors added, Sum of Sq how much the residual sum of squares went down, and F and Pr(>F) are the F-change and its p value.
You will often see all the models in one call:


Code
anova(m1, m2, m3)


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age
Model 2: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track + 
    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size
Model 3: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track + 
    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size + beauty
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    458 134.74                                  
2    454 124.21  4    10.537 10.140 7.201e-08 ***
3    453 117.69  1     6.521 25.101 7.813e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The last line is the same, but the F for step 2 is now 10.14 instead of 9.63. With several models, anova() divides every comparison by the unexplained variance of the largest model (here m3), not of the model at that step. Both are valid tests. The pairwise version matches the F-change formula and SPSS; say which one you report.


One predictor: ΔR² is its squared semipartial correlation
When a step adds a single predictor, two shortcuts hold:

\(\Delta R^2\) equals the squared semipartial correlation \(sr^2\): the squared correlation between the outcome and the part of beauty that the other eight predictors cannot predict.
The F-change equals the square of beauty’s t value in the final model.



Code
beauty_unique <- resid(lm(beauty ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track +
                            lower_division + single_credit + log2_size, data = d))   # beauty, minus what the others predict
t_beauty <- summary(m3)$coefficients["beauty", "t value"]
c(delta_r2 = steps$delta_r2[3], semipartial_squared = cor(d$eval, beauty_unique)^2,
  F_change = steps$F_change[3], t_squared = t_beauty^2)


           delta_r2 semipartial_squared            F_change           t_squared 
         0.04584582          0.04584582         25.10107854         25.10107854 


So \(\Delta R^2\) for a single predictor is the share of the variance of the evaluations that only beauty explains.

text:

summary(m3)



Call:

    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size + beauty, data = d)

How to read the output







Part
Meaning




Estimate
\(b\): the change in the evaluation for one unit more of the predictor, holding all the other predictors constant. For a 0/1 dummy, the difference between the two groups


Std. Error
How uncertain the estimate is


t value
Estimate / Std. Error


Pr(>|t|)
The chance of a t this large if the true effect were 0


Residual standard error
The typical distance of an evaluation from the model’s prediction, in evaluation points


Multiple R-squared, Adjusted R-squared
R² and adjusted R² of the final model, as in our table


F-statistic
Tests all nine predictors together against the model with none




(Intercept) is the predicted evaluation when every predictor is 0: a male, native, non-minority instructor aged 0, teaching one student. It is needed for the predictions but means nothing by itself.
beauty: 0.159 points per unit of beauty. One standard deviation of beauty (0.79) is worth 0.13 points, and the gap between the least and the best-looking instructor in the data is 0.55 points, about one standard deviation of the evaluations.
female: courses taught by women are rated 0.20 points lower than comparable courses taught by men.
single_credit: single-credit electives are rated 0.55 points higher.
log2_size: each doubling of the class costs 0.06 points.
non_native and minority instructors are rated 0.25 and 0.18 points lower; age, tenure track and division add nothing once the rest is held constant.

These are associations in observational data. Better-looking people may also be more confident or more practised speakers, so the coefficient says that beauty predicts evaluations, not that it causes them.


Standardised coefficients
The b’s are in different units (decades, doublings of the class, rating points), so they cannot be compared with each other. A standardised coefficient \(\beta\) puts every predictor in standard deviations: \(\beta = b \cdot \dfrac{SD_x}{SD_y}\), the change in the evaluation, in SDs, for one SD more of the predictor.


Code
sd_ratio <- sapply(d[predictors], sd) / sd(d$eval)
ci <- confint(m3)[predictors, ]
betas <- data.frame(predictor = factor(predictors, levels = rev(predictors)),
                    b = coef(m3)[predictors], beta = coef(m3)[predictors] * sd_ratio,
                    low = ci[, 1] * sd_ratio, high = ci[, 2] * sd_ratio)
round(betas[, -1], 3)

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
text:
6. The order matters
What if we had entered beauty first? Its share would then be its squared correlation with the evaluations. Entered last, it is its squared semipartial correlation. Here is that comparison for every predictor:


Code
full_r2 <- summary(m3)$r.squared
order_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(predictors, function(v) {
  alone   <- summary(lm(reformulate(v, "eval"), data = d))$r.squared            # entered first: r²
  without <- summary(update(m3, as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", v))))$r.squared
  data.frame(predictor = v, entered_first = alone, entered_last = full_r2 - without)   # entered last: sr²
}))
format(order_tab, digits = 2)


       predictor entered_first entered_last
1         female        0.0224      0.02708
2       minority        0.0059      0.01011
3     non_native        0.0200      0.01008
4            age        0.0027      0.00240
5   tenure_track        0.0168      0.00076
6 lower_division        0.0132      0.00072
7  single_credit        0.0553      0.04093
8      log2_size        0.0126      0.01496
9         beauty        0.0357      0.04585




Code
# (a) the same total R², credited differently in two orders
b1 <- lm(eval ~ beauty, data = d)
b2 <- update(b1, . ~ . + female + minority + non_native + age)
orders <- data.frame(
  order = factor(rep(c("planned order:\nbackground, course, beauty", "beauty first:\nbeauty, background, course"), each = 3),
                 levels = c("planned order:\nbackground, course, beauty", "beauty first:\nbeauty, background, course")),
  block = factor(rep(c("block 1: background", "block 2: course", "beauty"), 2),
                 levels = c("block 1: background", "block 2: course", "beauty")),
  value = c(steps$delta_r2,
            summary(b2)$r.squared - summary(b1)$r.squared, full_r2 - summary(b2)$r.squared, summary(b1)$r.squared),
  entry = c(1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 1))                     # the step at which each block enters: stacked in that order
pa <- ggplot(orders, aes(order, value, fill = block, group = entry)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", value)), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#f39c12", "#E74C3C")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "(a) The same total R², credited differently", x = NULL, y = "R²", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# (b) each predictor entered first (r²) and last (sr²)
order_tab$predictor <- factor(order_tab$predictor, levels = rev(predictors))
pb <- ggplot(order_tab, aes(y = predictor)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = entered_first, xend = entered_last, yend = predictor), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = entered_first, colour = "entered first (r²)"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = entered_last, colour = "entered last (sr²)"), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("entered first (r²)" = "#0082c8", "entered last (sr²)" = "#E74C3C")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "(b) Variance each predictor explains, entered first or last",
       x = "share of the variance of the evaluations", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
pa / pb









Two things happen:

Shared variance shrinks a predictor’s share. Tenure track explains 1.7% of the variance alone, but only 0.1% when entered last. What it explains, the other predictors explain too: tenure-track instructors rarely teach the well-rated single-credit electives (r = -0.29) and teach larger classes (r = 0.16). In hierarchical regression shared variance goes to the block that enters first. Division shows the same, because the single-credit electives are lower-division courses (r = 0.33), and so does native language.
Suppression enlarges it. Beauty explains 3.6% alone, but 4.6% entered last. Better-looking instructors are more often women (r = 0.13), teach somewhat larger classes (r = 0.07) and fewer single-credit electives (r = -0.08): all of these go with lower evaluations, so they hide part of beauty’s effect in the simple correlation. Holding them constant uncovers it. Gender, minority and class size grow for similar reasons.

That is why the order must be decided before the analysis and reported with the results: with correlated predictors, the credit each block gets depends on where it enters. The total R² does not change (panel a). Entering the predictor of interest last is the conservative choice: it gets credit only for what nothing else explains.

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
text:
7. Checking the assumptions
The F-change tests and the standard errors assume that the residuals have constant variance, are roughly normal, contain no extreme cases with undue influence, and are independent of each other; that the relationships are linear; and that the predictors are not too strongly correlated. report_regression() of the rwf package collects the usual checks for an lm model: diagnostic plots, standardised coefficients, VIFs, an outlier test and more. It also prints a long text report, which we capture here, and keep only the parts we need:


Code
set.seed(1)    # its Durbin-Watson test uses random resampling
invisible(capture.output(diag_m3 <- report_regression(m3, plot_diagnostics = TRUE)))

Here

No curve and no funnel shape
Flat, but the residuals are cut off at the top: no course can be rated above 5

A flat line: constant variance
Roughly flat

No case far above the others (values above 1 are a concern)
The largest is 0.05


Residuals vs Leverage, Cook’s dist vs Leverage
No case with both high leverage and a large residual
None

    rstudent            p   bonf.p signif cutoff
99 -3.591951 0.0003642181 0.168633  FALSE   0.05



Multicollinearity: the VIF (variance inflation factor) says how much a coefficient’s variance grows because the predictor correlates with the others. All are below 1.4, far from the usual warning level of 5 to 10.
Outliers: the most extreme residual is not significant after the Bonferroni correction (bonf.p = 0.17).
Normality: the skew comes from the ceiling at 5. With 463 cases, the tests of the coefficients are robust to it.

The assumption that these plots cannot check is independence, and these data break it.

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
section: 8. A caveat: 463 courses, but only 94 instructors
text:
8. A caveat: 463 courses, but only 94 instructors
Each instructor taught between 1 and 13 of the courses, and their beauty rating is the same in all of them. The plot shows every course as a point and joins the courses of the same instructor:


Code
ggplot(d, aes(beauty, eval, group = prof)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  labs(title = "Each vertical strip is one instructor and their courses",
       x = "beauty rating of the instructor", y = "course evaluation")









Courses of the same instructor are rated alike. The share of the unexplained variance that lies between instructors, the intraclass correlation of the residuals, is:


Code
d$residual <- resid(m3)
ri <- nlme::lme(residual ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | prof, data = d)   # residuals: instructor part + course part
vc <- as.numeric(nlme::VarCorr(ri)[, "Variance"])
icc <- vc[1] / sum(vc)
avg_courses <- n / length(unique(d$prof))
c(icc = icc, courses_per_instructor = avg_courses, design_effect = 1 + (avg_courses - 1) * icc)


                   icc courses_per_instructor          design_effect 
             0.4029194              4.9255319              2.5816729 


About 40% of what the model cannot explain is about who teaches the course. For a predictor that is constant within each instructor, like beauty, the 463 courses then carry about as much information as \(463 / \text{design effect} \approx\) 179 independent ones. Ordinary standard errors ignore this and are too small.
A quick fix is cluster-robust standard errors, which allow the residuals of the same instructor to be correlated:


Code
vc_cl <- vcovCL(m3, cluster = ~ prof)       # courses clustered within instructors
coeftest(m3, vcov = vc_cl)

The coefficients stay the same; the standard errors grow, for beauty from 0.032 to 0.049, close to what the design effect predicted (\(\sqrt{2.58}\) = 1.61 times larger). Beauty is still significant (p = 0.001), but minority (p = 0.072), non-native (p = 0.072) and class size (p = 0.095) are no longer significant at .05.
The F-change tests can be redone the same way with a Wald test, using the cluster-robust variance of the larger model:


Code
waldtest(m1, m2, vcov = vcovCL(m2, cluster = ~ prof))   # step 2


Wald test

    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size

Model 1: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track + 
    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size
Model 2: eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track + 
    lower_division + single_credit + log2_size + beauty
  Res.Df Df      F   Pr(>F)

2    453  1 10.783 0.001104 **
