Beauty’s robust F = 10.78 is its robust t squared (3.28²), against 25.1 with ordinary standard errors. The R² changes stay as they were; only their tests change.
Cluster-robust errors fix the standard errors, but they do not model the instructors. A multilevel model with a random intercept for each instructor does both, and also tells how much instructors differ: see the Multilevel Models tutorial.

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
section: 9. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
9. Reporting the results in APA style
A hierarchical regression report (APA 7th edition) gives the order of the blocks and why, R², \(\Delta R^2\) and the F-change of every step, and the coefficients of the final model. We collect the numbers from the R objects:


Code
f2d  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
s3   <- summary(m3)$coefficients
cl   <- coeftest(m3, vcov = vc_cl)


Method (data analysis):

Course evaluations were analysed with a three-step hierarchical regression. Instructor characteristics (gender, minority status, native English, age) were entered in Step 1, job and course characteristics (tenure track, lower division, single-credit course, class size as the base-2 logarithm of enrolment) in Step 2, and the instructor’s beauty rating in Step 3, so that beauty was credited only with variance not explained by the other predictors. Because the 463 courses were taught by 94 instructors, we also report standard errors clustered by instructor. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the sandwich and lmtest packages.

Results:

Instructor characteristics explained 5.3% of the variance in evaluations, R² = .05, F(4, 458) = 6.37, p < .001. Job and course characteristics explained an additional 7.4%, ΔR² = .07, F(4, 454) = 9.63, p < .001. Adding beauty in Step 3 increased the explained variance by a further 4.6%, ΔR² = .05, F(1, 453) = 25.10, p < .001, f² = .06. In the final model, R² = .17, adjusted R² = .16, more attractive instructors received higher evaluations, b = 0.16, SE = 0.03, β = .23, p < .001: one standard deviation of beauty was associated with 0.13 points higher evaluations on the 5-point scale. The effect remained significant with standard errors clustered by instructor, SE = 0.05, p = .001.

Points to remember:

Give the order of the blocks and the reason for it, decided before the analysis.
Report R² for every step, and for every block \(\Delta R^2\) with its F-change, degrees of freedom and p; an effect size such as \(f^2\) for the step of interest helps.
Say which F you report when you use anova() with more than two models (section 4).
Report the coefficients of the final model (and, if useful, of every step, as in Table 1), with b, SE and, for continuous predictors, β.
Say how you handled any dependence in the data, such as several observations per person or group.
Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("sandwich") in R give the exact references.

title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
text:
10. Summary







What it answers
Does a predictor (or block) explain variance over and above others: incremental validity


How
Enter blocks in an order fixed in advance by theory; test each step with ΔR² and its F-change


ΔR²
\(R^2_2 - R^2_1\); for a single predictor, its squared semipartial correlation


F-change
\(F = \dfrac{\Delta R^2 / \Delta k}{(1 - R^2_2) / (n - k_2 - 1)}\); in R, anova(m1, m2) for each pair


Effect size
\(f^2 = \Delta R^2 / (1 - R^2_2)\): .02 small, .15 medium, .35 large


The order matters
Shared variance goes to the block that enters first; suppression can make a later predictor explain more. Put the predictor of interest last


Not stepwise
You choose the order, not the p values


Same cases
Every model must use the same rows: remove missing values first


Dependence
Several observations per person or group: cluster-robust SEs (sandwich::vcovCL) or a multilevel model


Here
Beauty added 4.6% of explained variance after eight other predictors; one SD of beauty ≈ 0.13 evaluation points

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
A company surveys 1,000 employees about their weekly working hours, their sleep quality and their wellbeing. We want two numbers: the average wellbeing, and how much wellbeing goes down with every extra hour of work. But 30% of the employees skipped the wellbeing page, and 10% did not give their hours.
What happens next depends on why the answers are missing. Rubin (1976) named three cases:








Mechanism
In words
In the survey




MCAR: missing completely at random
Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with any variable
A batch of questionnaires was lost in the post


MAR: missing at random
Whether a value is missing depends on other, observed variables
People who sleep badly skip the wellbeing page more often, and we know their sleep


MNAR: missing not at random
Whether a value is missing depends on the missing value itself
People with low wellbeing skip the wellbeing page, because of their low wellbeing



The names are confusing: “missing at random” does not mean random. It means random once we take the observed variables into account: among people with the same sleep quality, who skipped the page is random.
Most software, R included, handles missing values by quietly dropping every incomplete row (listwise deletion). This page shows when that is harmless, when it is not, why the popular quick fixes are worse, and how multiple imputation does better. Because we simulate the data, we know the true answers and can check every method against them.


Code
library(mice)       # multiple imputation by chained equations
library(MASS)       # mvrnorm(): correlated normal data
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
1. Simulate the complete data
Hours, sleep quality and wellbeing are drawn from a multivariate normal distribution with these means, standard deviations and correlations:



Variable
Mean
SD
Correlation with hours
with sleep




hours (per week)
40
8




sleep (quality, 0 to 10)
6
1.5
−0.20



wellbeing (0 to 100)
60

−0.30
0.60





Code
means <- c(hours = 40, sleep = 6, wellbeing = 60)
sds   <- c(hours = 8, sleep = 1.5, wellbeing = 12)
corr  <- matrix(c( 1.00, -0.20, -0.30,
                  -0.20,  1.00,  0.60,
                  -0.30,  0.60,  1.00), 3, dimnames = list(names(means), names(means)))
Sigma <- diag(sds) %*% corr %*% diag(sds)          # the covariance matrix
dimnames(Sigma) <- dimnames(corr)

true_mean  <- 60
true_slope <- unname(corr["hours", "wellbeing"] * sds["wellbeing"] / sds["hours"])   # r * SD_y / SD_x
true_slope


[1] -0.45


Code
make_people <- function(n) as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n, means, Sigma))
set.seed(2026)
full <- make_people(1000)
fit_full <- lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = full)
c(mean_wellbeing = mean(full$wellbeing), slope = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"]))


mean_wellbeing          slope 
    59.7983421     -0.4648238 


In the population, wellbeing drops by 0.45 points per extra hour of work (\(b = r \times SD_y / SD_x = -0.30 \times 12 / 8\)). Our sample of 1,000 gives 59.80 and -0.465: these are the answers we would get without missing data, the benchmark for every method below.
Sleep is not part of our question. It plays the role of an auxiliary variable: measured in the same survey, related to wellbeing, and (section 5) very useful.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
2. Three ways to lose data
The function below removes about 30% of the wellbeing values, in one of the three ways, and 10% of the hours completely at random:

MCAR: 300 wellbeing values chosen at random, with generate_missing() of the rwf package.
MAR: the chance of missing wellbeing depends on sleep: \(P(\text{missing}) = \text{logistic}(a - 1.5\,z_{\text{sleep}})\), where \(z\) is the standardised sleep score and \(a\) is set to give 30% missing. People who sleep badly skip it more often.
MNAR: the same, but with \(z_{\text{wellbeing}}\): the lower the wellbeing, the more likely it is missing.



Code
add_missing <- function(complete, mechanism, share = 0.30) {
  d <- complete
  n <- nrow(d)
  z <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
  p_missing <- function(lp) {                         # choose the intercept a that gives the wanted share
    a <- uniroot(function(a) mean(plogis(a + lp)) - share, c(-10, 10))$root
    plogis(a + lp)
  }
  if (mechanism == "MCAR") d$wellbeing <- generate_missing(d$wellbeing, missing = round(share * n))
  if (mechanism == "MAR")  d$wellbeing[runif(n) < p_missing(-1.5 * z(d$sleep))] <- NA
  if (mechanism == "MNAR") d$wellbeing[runif(n) < p_missing(-1.5 * z(d$wellbeing))] <- NA
  d$hours <- generate_missing(d$hours, missing = round(0.10 * n))   # 10% of hours: completely at random
  d
}

set.seed(1)
data_mcar <- add_missing(full, "MCAR")
data_mar  <- add_missing(full, "MAR")
data_mnar <- add_missing(full, "MNAR")


In real data we never see the missing values. Here we do, so we can look at who went missing:


Code
mech <- rbind(data.frame(full, missing = is.na(data_mcar$wellbeing), mechanism = "MCAR: at random"),
              data.frame(full, missing = is.na(data_mar$wellbeing),  mechanism = "MAR: depends on sleep"),
              data.frame(full, missing = is.na(data_mnar$wellbeing), mechanism = "MNAR: depends on wellbeing"))
mech$mechanism <- factor(mech$mechanism, levels = unique(mech$mechanism))
ggplot(mech, aes(sleep, wellbeing, colour = missing)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~mechanism) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#0082c8", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"), labels = c("observed", "missing")) +
  labs(title = "Which wellbeing values went missing", x = "sleep quality", y = "wellbeing", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










MCAR: the red points are scattered everywhere.
MAR: they gather on the left, among people who sleep badly. Since bad sleepers also have lower wellbeing, the missing values are mostly low ones.
MNAR: they gather at the bottom: the low wellbeing values themselves are missing.

What happens if we simply analyse the observed values?


Code
round(sapply(list(complete = full, MCAR = data_mcar, MAR = data_mar, MNAR = data_mnar), function(d)
  c(share_missing  = mean(is.na(d$wellbeing)),
    mean_wellbeing = mean(d$wellbeing, na.rm = TRUE),
    slope          = unname(coef(lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = d))["hours"]))), 3)


               complete   MCAR    MAR   MNAR
share_missing     0.000  0.300  0.323  0.318
mean_wellbeing   59.798 59.757 62.145 63.878
slope            -0.465 -0.505 -0.409 -0.373


Under MCAR the observed values are a random subset, so the estimates are fine, only less precise. Under MAR and MNAR the people who stayed are happier than the people who left, so the average wellbeing is too high, and the slope is too flat.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 3. Look at the missing data first
text:
3. Look at the missing data first

The missing-data pattern
md.pattern() counts the combinations of observed and missing values:


Code
md.pattern(data_mar, plot = FALSE)


    sleep hours wellbeing    
608     1     1         1   0
292     1     1         0   1
69      1     0         1   1
31      1     0         0   2
        0   100       323 423


How to read it: each row is a pattern, with 1 for observed and 0 for missing. The row name is the number of people with that pattern, and the last column the number of missing values in it. The last row gives the number of missing values per variable. Here 608 people answered everything, and 392 (39%) have at least one hole, so listwise deletion would drop more than a third of the sample. The same pattern as a picture:


Code
pat <- md.pattern(data_mar, plot = FALSE)
counts <- as.numeric(rownames(pat)[-nrow(pat)])
tiles <- expand.grid(pattern = seq_along(counts), variable = colnames(pat)[-ncol(pat)])
tiles$observed <- as.vector(pat[-nrow(pat), -ncol(pat)]) == 1
tiles$label <- factor(paste0(counts, " people")[tiles$pattern], levels = rev(paste0(counts, " people")))
ggplot(tiles, aes(variable, label, fill = observed)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#0082c8", `FALSE` = "#E74C3C"), labels = c("missing", "observed")) +
  labs(title = "Missing-data patterns (MAR data)", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL)











Is it MCAR?
We can check whether missingness is related to observed variables: a logistic regression of “wellbeing is missing” on sleep.


Code
missing_vs_sleep <- function(d) summary(glm(is.na(wellbeing) ~ sleep, family = binomial, data = d))$coefficients["sleep", ]
round(rbind(MCAR = missing_vs_sleep(data_mcar), MAR = missing_vs_sleep(data_mar), MNAR = missing_vs_sleep(data_mnar)), 4)


     Estimate Std. Error  z value Pr(>|z|)
MCAR  -0.0287     0.0464  -0.6186   0.5362
MAR   -1.0246     0.0742 -13.8029   0.0000
MNAR  -0.5264     0.0546  -9.6483   0.0000


Under MCAR sleep does not predict missingness. Under MAR it does strongly, so the data are not MCAR. But look at the MNAR row: sleep predicts missingness there too, because sleep is correlated with the wellbeing that drives it. No test can tell MAR from MNAR, because the difference lies in the values we do not have. That choice rests on knowledge of how the data were collected, and on the sensitivity analysis of section 6.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 4. The quick fixes, and what they do
text:
4. The quick fixes, and what they do
From here on we use the MAR data, the realistic case. Four common approaches:

Listwise deletion: analyse only the complete rows (R’s default).
Mean imputation: fill each hole with the mean of the variable.
Regression imputation: fill each hole with the value predicted from the other variables.
Stochastic regression imputation: the same, plus a random error, so the imputed values scatter like real ones.

mice() can do all three imputations once (m = 1), with method = "mean", "norm.predict" and "norm.nob":


Code
single <- function(method) complete(mice(data_mar, m = 1, method = method, maxit = if (method == "mean") 1 else 5,
                                         printFlag = FALSE, seed = 1))
filled <- list("complete data (benchmark)" = full,
               "listwise deletion"         = na.omit(data_mar),
               "mean imputation"           = single("mean"),
               "regression imputation"     = single("norm.predict"),
               "stochastic regression"     = single("norm.nob"))
describe_fit <- function(d) {
  f <- lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = d)
  c(n = nobs(f), mean = mean(d$wellbeing), sd = sd(d$wellbeing), r = cor(d$hours, d$wellbeing),
    slope = unname(coef(f)["hours"]), se = summary(f)$coefficients["hours", "Std. Error"])
}
quick <- t(sapply(filled, describe_fit))
round(quick, 3)


                             n   mean     sd      r  slope    se
complete data (benchmark) 1000 59.798 11.910 -0.301 -0.465 0.047
listwise deletion          608 62.414 11.175 -0.277 -0.409 0.058
mean imputation           1000 62.145  9.298 -0.211 -0.267 0.039
regression imputation     1000 59.705 10.546 -0.363 -0.518 0.042
stochastic regression     1000 59.867 11.839 -0.316 -0.483 0.046




Code
shown <- c("mean imputation", "regression imputation", "stochastic regression")
pts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(shown, function(nm)
  data.frame(filled[[nm]][, c("hours", "wellbeing")], imputed = is.na(data_mar$wellbeing), method = nm)))
pts$method <- factor(pts$method, levels = shown)
ggplot(pts, aes(hours, wellbeing, colour = imputed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~method) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#0082c8", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"), labels = c("observed", "imputed")) +
  labs(title = "Where the imputed wellbeing values land", x = "weekly hours", y = "wellbeing", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Row by row:

Listwise deletion keeps 608 of 1,000 people. Its mean (62.41) is too high, because the bad sleepers, who are less happy, are the ones who left.
Mean imputation is the worst. Every hole gets the same value: the horizontal red line in the plot, and the vertical blue line of people whose hours were filled with the mean. So the mean stays as biased as with deletion, the SD shrinks (9.30 against 11.91), and the correlation and slope are pulled towards 0 (-0.267). On top of that, R treats the 1,000 rows as real data, so the standard error is too small.
Regression imputation uses sleep, so the mean is nearly right. But each imputed value is an exact prediction from hours and sleep, with none of the scatter of real data around the prediction, so in the middle plot the red points are packed more tightly than the blue ones. The SD is too small, the correlation too strong (-0.363 against -0.301), and the standard error too small.
Stochastic regression adds random scatter, so the mean, SD, correlation and slope all come out about right. Only the standard error is still wrong: R thinks the imputed values are as certain as observed ones, but they are guesses. The next section fixes that.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
5. Multiple imputation
Multiple imputation (Rubin, 1987) does stochastic imputation not once but \(m\) times, creating \(m\) complete datasets that differ only in the imputed values. Each dataset is analysed as usual, and the \(m\) results are combined. The differences between the \(m\) results show how uncertain the imputations are, and that uncertainty goes into the standard errors.
mice (multivariate imputation by chained equations; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) imputes one variable at a time from all the others, cycling through the variables a few times. Its default for numeric variables is predictive mean matching (pmm): for each missing value it predicts a value from the other variables, finds the five observed cases whose predictions are closest, and borrows the real value of one of them at random. The imputed values are therefore always values that really occur in the data.


Code
imp <- mice(data_mar, m = 40, method = "pmm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
imp


Class: mids
Number of multiple imputations:  40 
Imputation methods:
    hours     sleep wellbeing 
    "pmm"        ""     "pmm" 
PredictorMatrix:
          hours sleep wellbeing
hours         0     1         1
sleep         1     0         1
wellbeing     1     1         0


How to read it:

Number of multiple imputations: \(m\) = 40 completed datasets (why 40: see below).
Imputation methods: pmm for the two incomplete variables; "" for sleep, which has nothing to impute.
PredictorMatrix: which variables (columns) predict which (rows). By default every variable predicts every other. Include the variables of the analysis (the outcome too), and auxiliary variables such as sleep.

Analyse each completed dataset with with(), and combine with pool():


Code
fits   <- with(imp, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))
pooled <- pool(fits)
summary(pooled, conf.int = TRUE)


         term   estimate  std.error statistic       df      p.value      2.5 %     97.5 %   conf.low  conf.high
1 (Intercept) 78.0165217 2.41001487 32.371801 175.4128 6.810418e-76 73.2601643 82.7728791 73.2601643 82.7728791
2       hours -0.4548743 0.06113269 -7.440771 150.5196 7.120770e-12 -0.5756633 -0.3340853 -0.5756633 -0.3340853


Code
pooled_mean <- summary(pool(with(imp, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))), conf.int = TRUE)   # the mean of wellbeing
pooled_mean


         term estimate std.error statistic      df       p.value    2.5 %   97.5 % conf.low conf.high
1 (Intercept) 59.81394 0.4377225  136.6481 295.041 8.576632e-269 58.95248 60.67539 58.95248  60.67539


The columns are read like a regression table: estimate, std.error, statistic (t), df, p.value and the 95% confidence interval. The pooled mean of wellbeing is 59.81, against 59.80 in the complete data and 62.41 after listwise deletion.

Rubin’s rules, by hand
With \(m\) estimates \(\hat Q_1, \dots, \hat Q_m\) and their squared standard errors \(U_1, \dots, U_m\):

Pooled estimate: the average, \(\bar Q = \frac{1}{m}\sum \hat Q_j\)
Within-imputation variance: the average squared standard error, \(\bar U = \frac{1}{m}\sum U_j\). The uncertainty we would have if the data were complete.
Between-imputation variance: the variance of the estimates, \(B = \frac{1}{m-1}\sum (\hat Q_j - \bar Q)^2\). The extra uncertainty caused by the missing values.
Total variance: \(T = \bar U + \left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right) B\), and the pooled standard error is \(\sqrt{T}\).

Three summaries of how much the missing data cost:

Relative increase in variance: \(r = \dfrac{(1 + 1/m)\,B}{\bar U}\)
Proportion of variance due to missingness: \(\lambda = \dfrac{(1 + 1/m)\,B}{T}\)
Fraction of missing information: \(\text{FMI} = \dfrac{r + 2/(\nu + 3)}{r + 1}\), where \(\nu\) is the degrees of freedom (Barnard & Rubin, 1999).



Code
est <- sapply(fits$analyses, function(f) coef(f)[["hours"]])
u   <- sapply(fits$analyses, function(f) vcov(f)["hours", "hours"])
m   <- length(est)
q_bar  <- mean(est)
u_bar  <- mean(u)
b      <- var(est)
t_var  <- u_bar + (1 + 1 / m) * b
riv    <- (1 + 1 / m) * b / u_bar
lambda <- (1 + 1 / m) * b / t_var
df_com <- nrow(data_mar) - 2                                    # the df if the data were complete
df_old <- (m - 1) / lambda^2
df_obs <- (df_com + 1) / (df_com + 3) * df_com * (1 - lambda)
df     <- df_old * df_obs / (df_old + df_obs)                   # Barnard-Rubin degrees of freedom
fmi    <- (riv + 2 / (df + 3)) / (riv + 1)
by_hand <- c(estimate = q_bar, ubar = u_bar, b = b, t = t_var, df = df, riv = riv, lambda = lambda, fmi = fmi)
from_pool <- unlist(pooled$pooled[pooled$pooled$term == "hours", names(by_hand)])
signif(rbind(by_hand, from_pool), 4)


          estimate     ubar        b        t    df    riv lambda    fmi
by_hand    -0.4549 0.002109 0.001588 0.003737 150.5 0.7717 0.4356 0.4429
from_pool  -0.4549 0.002109 0.001588 0.003737 150.5 0.7717 0.4356 0.4429


The two rows agree. For the slope, \(\lambda\) = 0.44: about 44% of its variance comes from not knowing the missing values, and the FMI says about 44% of the information about it was lost.
The FMI is not simply the share of missing values. The better the other variables predict the missing values, the smaller it is: with a perfect predictor nothing would be lost. Sleep predicts wellbeing only moderately (r = 0.60), and here the FMI ends up a little above the share of people with an incomplete row (39%).


Checking the imputations
Convergence. mice iterates; the mean of the imputed values should settle down and the separate runs (chains) should mix, with no trend:


Code
imp_trace <- mice(data_mar, m = 5, maxit = 20, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
chains <- imp_trace$chainMean["wellbeing", , ]                    # iterations x chains
trace_df <- data.frame(iteration = rep(seq_len(nrow(chains)), ncol(chains)), chain = factor(rep(seq_len(ncol(chains)), each = nrow(chains))),
                       mean = as.vector(chains))
c1 <- ggplot(trace_df, aes(iteration, mean, colour = chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Convergence of the\nimputed mean", x = "iteration", y = "mean of imputed wellbeing") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

imputed <- imp$imp$wellbeing                                     # one column per imputation
dens <- rbind(data.frame(value = data_mar$wellbeing[!is.na(data_mar$wellbeing)], set = "observed", draw = "0"),
              data.frame(value = unlist(imputed), set = "imputed", draw = rep(names(imputed), each = nrow(imputed))))
c2 <- ggplot(dens, aes(value, group = draw, colour = set, linewidth = set)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(observed = "#0082c8", imputed = "#E74C3C")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(observed = 1.4, imputed = 0.2)) +
  labs(title = "Observed and imputed wellbeing\n(one red line per imputation)", x = "wellbeing", y = "density",
       colour = NULL, linewidth = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
c1 + c2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.3))










Left: the chains wander around the same level from the first iterations, with no trend. Five iterations (the default) are enough here.
Right: the imputed values (red) lie lower than the observed ones (blue). That is not a fault. Under MAR the people with missing wellbeing sleep worse, so their wellbeing is expected to be lower. A difference between observed and imputed values is a problem only if it makes no sense; impossible values (say, below 0) would be one.



How many imputations?
The old advice was 5. With 5, the results change noticeably every time you run the imputation with another seed. A useful rule is to use at least as many imputations as the percentage of incomplete cases (White et al., 2011): here 39%, so about 40. The spread of the pooled slope and its standard error over 10 runs with different seeds:


Code
spread <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(5, 20, 40), function(mm) do.call(rbind, lapply(1:10, function(s) {
  p <- summary(pool(with(mice(data_mar, m = mm, seed = s, printFlag = FALSE), lm(wellbeing ~ hours))))
  data.frame(m = mm, estimate = p$estimate[2], se = p$std.error[2])
}))))
round(do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spread, spread$m), function(s)
  c(m = s$m[1], estimate_mean = mean(s$estimate), estimate_sd = sd(s$estimate),
    se_mean = mean(s$se), se_sd = sd(s$se)))), 4)


    m estimate_mean estimate_sd se_mean  se_sd
5   5       -0.4681      0.0146  0.0599 0.0097
20 20       -0.4635      0.0080  0.0576 0.0034
40 40       -0.4619      0.0055  0.0579 0.0021


The averages hardly change, but the run-to-run spread (estimate_sd, se_sd) shrinks as \(m\) grows. With 40 imputations a second run would give practically the same numbers.


Auxiliary variables
The data are MAR given sleep. What if we leave sleep out of the imputation model?


Code
imp_no_aux <- mice(data_mar[, c("hours", "wellbeing")], m = 40, method = "pmm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
mi_summary <- function(im) c(mean  = summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))))$estimate,
                             slope = summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))))$estimate[2])
aux <- rbind("complete data (benchmark)" = c(mean = mean(full$wellbeing), slope = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"])),
             "listwise deletion"         = quick["listwise deletion", c("mean", "slope")],
             "MI without sleep"          = mi_summary(imp_no_aux),
             "MI with sleep"             = mi_summary(imp))
round(aux, 3)


                            mean  slope
complete data (benchmark) 59.798 -0.465
listwise deletion         62.414 -0.409
MI without sleep          61.949 -0.406
MI with sleep             59.814 -0.455


Without sleep, multiple imputation is no better than deletion: from the point of view of a model that does not know sleep, the data are not MAR. With sleep, it recovers the benchmark. So put in the imputation model every variable that predicts the missing values or the missingness, even if it is not part of the analysis (the “inclusive strategy”; Collins et al., 2001).
The same holds for any analysis that compares models: every step of a Hierarchical Regression must use the same people, which multiple imputation gives you without dropping anyone. Fit each step in each imputed dataset and pool them; for example pool.r.squared(fits) pools \(R^2\):


Code
pool.r.squared(fits)


           est      lo 95     hi 95       fmi
R^2 0.08949307 0.05018298 0.1374607 0.4134909

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 6. MNAR: when imputation is not enough
text:
6. MNAR: when imputation is not enough
Multiple imputation assumes MAR. With the MNAR data:


Code
imp_mnar <- mice(data_mnar, m = 40, method = "pmm", seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
mnar_tab <- rbind("complete data (benchmark)" = c(mean = mean(full$wellbeing), slope = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"])),
                  "listwise deletion"         = c(mean = mean(na.omit(data_mnar)$wellbeing),
                                                  slope = unname(coef(lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = data_mnar))["hours"])),
                  "multiple imputation"       = mi_summary(imp_mnar))
round(mnar_tab, 3)


                            mean  slope
complete data (benchmark) 59.798 -0.465
listwise deletion         64.054 -0.373
multiple imputation       62.552 -0.406


Imputation helps a little, because sleep carries some information about the missing wellbeing values, but the mean is still too high. The data cannot tell us how much lower the missing values are.
What we can do is a sensitivity analysis: ask how the results change if the missing people are worse off than MAR predicts. The delta adjustment (van Buuren, 2018) subtracts a fixed amount \(\delta\) from every imputed wellbeing value, through the post argument of mice():


Code
deltas <- c(0, -2, -4, -6, -8, -10)
sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(deltas, function(delta) {
  post <- make.post(data_mnar)
  post["wellbeing"] <- paste("imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] +", delta)      # shift every imputed value by delta
  im <- mice(data_mnar, m = 20, method = "pmm", post = post, seed = 2026, printFlag = FALSE)
  pm <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))), conf.int = TRUE)
  ps <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))), conf.int = TRUE)
  data.frame(delta, mean = pm$estimate, mean_low = pm$`2.5 %`, mean_high = pm$`97.5 %`,
             slope = ps$estimate[2], slope_low = ps$`2.5 %`[2], slope_high = ps$`97.5 %`[2])
}))
round(sens, 3)


  delta   mean mean_low mean_high  slope slope_low slope_high
1     0 62.479   61.738    63.220 -0.407    -0.514     -0.300
2    -2 61.792   60.991    62.592 -0.431    -0.537     -0.325
3    -4 61.212   60.460    61.964 -0.442    -0.554     -0.330
4    -6 60.538   59.709    61.367 -0.472    -0.585     -0.358
5    -8 59.933   59.082    60.783 -0.481    -0.599     -0.363
6   -10 59.273   58.399    60.146 -0.519    -0.643     -0.395




Code
s1 <- ggplot(sens, aes(delta, mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(full$wellbeing), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_low, ymax = mean_high), fill = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Mean wellbeing", x = "delta (shift of the imputed values)", y = "pooled estimate, 95% CI")
s2 <- ggplot(sens, aes(delta, slope)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = unname(coef(fit_full)["hours"]), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = slope_low, ymax = slope_high), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(colour = "#E74C3C", linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(colour = "#E74C3C", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Slope of hours", x = "delta (shift of the imputed values)", y = NULL)
s1 + s2 + plot_annotation(caption = "Dashed line: the complete-data value, which real data never show")









As \(\delta\) grows, the estimated mean falls, and somewhere around \(\delta\) = -8 it reaches the complete-data value (which in real life we would not know). The slope moves less and stays clearly negative for every \(\delta\) tried.
In practice, report the analysis under MAR and then the range of results for plausible values of \(\delta\), chosen with subject knowledge (for example, “people who skip a wellbeing page score up to 5 points lower than similar people who answer it”). If the conclusion survives the whole range, it is robust; if it flips at some \(\delta\), say where.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
7. A simulation: bias and coverage
One dataset can be lucky. We repeat everything 100 times for each mechanism (500 people per sample) and record, for every method, the average error of the estimates (bias) and how often its 95% confidence interval contains the true value (coverage, which should be 95%). The truth is the population value: a mean of 60 and a slope of -0.45. To keep the page fast, multiple imputation uses 5 imputations here.


Code
ci_lm <- function(f, term) {
  e <- coef(f)[[term]]; se <- summary(f)$coefficients[term, "Std. Error"]; q <- qt(0.975, df.residual(f))
  c(estimate = e, low = e - q * se, high = e + q * se)
}
both <- function(d) rbind(mean = ci_lm(lm(wellbeing ~ 1, data = d), "(Intercept)"),
                          slope = ci_lm(lm(wellbeing ~ hours, data = d), "hours"))
one_run <- function(mechanism, n = 500) {
  d <- add_missing(make_people(n), mechanism)
  out <- list("listwise deletion"     = both(na.omit(d)),
              "mean imputation"       = both(complete(mice(d, m = 1, maxit = 1, method = "mean", printFlag = FALSE))),
              "regression imputation" = both(complete(mice(d, m = 1, method = "norm.predict", printFlag = FALSE))),
              "stochastic regression" = both(complete(mice(d, m = 1, method = "norm.nob", printFlag = FALSE))))
  im <- mice(d, m = 5, method = "pmm", printFlag = FALSE)
  pm <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ 1))), conf.int = TRUE)
  ps <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(wellbeing ~ hours))), conf.int = TRUE)
  out[["multiple imputation"]] <- rbind(mean  = c(pm$estimate, pm$`2.5 %`, pm$`97.5 %`),
                                        slope = c(ps$estimate[2], ps$`2.5 %`[2], ps$`97.5 %`[2]))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(out), function(nm) data.frame(mechanism, method = nm, estimand = c("mean", "slope"),
                                                            estimate = out[[nm]][, 1], low = out[[nm]][, 2], high = out[[nm]][, 3])))
}
set.seed(11)
sim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"), function(mech) do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_run(mech), simplify = FALSE))))
sim$truth   <- ifelse(sim$estimand == "mean", true_mean, true_slope)
sim$covered <- sim$low <= sim$truth & sim$truth <= sim$high
res <- aggregate(cbind(bias = estimate - truth, coverage = covered) ~ mechanism + method + estimand, data = sim, FUN = mean)
res$mechanism <- factor(res$mechanism, levels = c("MCAR", "MAR", "MNAR"))
res$method <- factor(res$method, levels = rev(c("listwise deletion", "mean imputation", "regression imputation",
                                                "stochastic regression", "multiple imputation")))
res <- res[order(res$estimand, res$mechanism, -as.integer(res$method)), ]
rownames(res) <- NULL
res

# one number from the table, for the text below
get <- function(mech, meth, est, what) res[res$mechanism == mech & res$method == meth & res$estimand == est, what]




Code
long <- rbind(data.frame(res[, c("mechanism", "method")], panel = paste("Bias of the", res$estimand), value = res$bias),
              data.frame(res[, c("mechanism", "method")], panel = paste("Coverage of the", res$estimand), value = res$coverage))
long$panel <- factor(long$panel, levels = c("Bias of the mean", "Bias of the slope", "Coverage of the mean", "Coverage of the slope"))
refs <- data.frame(panel = factor(levels(long$panel), levels = levels(long$panel)), x = c(0, 0, 0.95, 0.95))
ggplot(long, aes(value, method, colour = mechanism)) +
  geom_vline(data = refs, aes(xintercept = x), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.8, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(MCAR = "#0082c8", MAR = "#f39c12", MNAR = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "100 samples per mechanism: average error and 95% CI coverage\n(dashed: no bias, 95% coverage)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "lines"))









What the simulation shows (the true slope is negative, so a positive bias of the slope means a slope that is too flat):

Listwise deletion is fine under MCAR: no bias, and coverage of 0.97 for the mean and 0.90 for the slope (with 100 samples, coverage is itself uncertain by about ±0.04). Under MAR and MNAR its mean is too high, by 2.4 and 3.9 points, and its intervals almost never contain the true mean.
Mean imputation pulls the slope towards 0 even under MCAR (a bias of 0.14), and its intervals contain the true slope only 31% of the time or less.
Regression imputation gets the mean nearly right under MAR, but makes the slope too steep (a bias of -0.05), and its intervals are too narrow (coverage of the slope 0.79).
Stochastic regression is about as accurate as multiple imputation here, since the simulated data are exactly normal, which suits it. But its intervals are too narrow, because one imputation hides the uncertainty of the guesses: coverage between 0.89 and 0.94 under MCAR and MAR.
Multiple imputation is nearly unbiased under MCAR and MAR (for the mean under MAR, 0.20 points, against 2.42 for deletion), with coverage between 0.91 and 0.97. Under MNAR every method is biased; only a sensitivity analysis (section 6) shows how much it could matter.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
section: 8. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
8. Reporting the results in APA style
A report should give the amount and pattern of missing data, the assumed mechanism and why, how the imputation was done, and the pooled results (Enders, 2022; van Buuren, 2018). We collect the numbers from the R objects:


Code
sp  <- summary(pooled, conf.int = TRUE)
row <- sp[sp$term == "hours", ]
pf  <- pooled$pooled[pooled$pooled$term == "hours", ]
mis_test <- missing_vs_sleep(data_mar)

f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))


Method (missing data):

Of the 1,000 participants, 32.3% had missing wellbeing scores and 10% missing working hours; 39.2% had at least one missing value. Missing wellbeing was more likely among participants reporting poorer sleep quality, b = -1.02, p < .001, so the data were not missing completely at random. We assumed that they were missing at random given the observed variables, and handled them with multiple imputation by chained equations in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the mice package (Version 3.19.0; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011). Missing values were imputed with predictive mean matching, using wellbeing, working hours and sleep quality (an auxiliary variable) as predictors. We created 40 imputed datasets, analysed each separately, and combined the results with Rubin’s rules.

Results:

Across the imputed datasets, mean wellbeing was 59.81, 95% CI [58.95, 60.68]. Each additional weekly working hour was associated with lower wellbeing, b = -0.45, SE = 0.06, t(150.5) = -7.44, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.58, -0.33]. The fraction of missing information for this coefficient was .44.

Points to remember:

Report how much is missing, per variable and in total (the share of incomplete cases), and the main patterns.
Say which mechanism you assume and why, and what you checked (which observed variables predict missingness).
Describe the imputation model: the method, the number of imputations and iterations, and all the variables in it, auxiliary ones included.
Report pooled estimates with their standard errors or confidence intervals; the FMI shows how much the missing data cost.
If MNAR is plausible, add a sensitivity analysis, such as the delta adjustment, and report how far the conclusions hold.
Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("mice") in R give the exact references.

title: Missing Data and Multiple Imputation in R With mice
text:
9. Summary







MCAR
Missingness unrelated to anything: deletion is unbiased, only less precise


MAR
Missingness depends on observed variables: deletion is biased; multiple imputation that uses those variables is not


MNAR
Missingness depends on the missing values: no method fixes it from the data alone; use a sensitivity analysis


Telling them apart
Observed variables that predict missingness rule out MCAR; nothing in the data can rule out MNAR


Mean imputation
Never: shrinks variances, distorts correlations, too-small standard errors


Regression imputation
Imputed values on a line: correlations too strong, standard errors too small


One stochastic imputation
Estimates fine, standard errors too small


Multiple imputation
imp <- mice(d, m = 40); pool(with(imp, lm(...))): valid estimates and standard errors under MAR


Rubin’s rules
\(T = \bar U + (1 + 1/m)B\); FMI = the share of information lost


How many imputations
At least the percentage of incomplete cases


Imputation model
All analysis variables, the outcome included, plus auxiliary variables


Check
Convergence of the chains; imputed values that make sense

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
In 1982 the High School and Beyond survey gave a mathematics test to students of US high schools, public and Catholic. We use the classic subset of 7,185 students in 160 schools, and ask two questions:

Students from richer families score higher in maths. Is that gap the same in every school?
Do school characteristics, such as being a Catholic school or having richer students on average, change the scores and the gap?

The students are not 7,185 independent people. They come in groups: students of the same school share teachers, neighbourhoods and resources, so their scores are more alike than the scores of students from different schools. Ordinary regression ignores this, which causes two problems:

Wrong standard errors. Ordinary regression treats every student as new information, so it is far too confident about anything measured at the school level (section 4).
The wrong question. Ordinary regression gives one slope for everyone. The interesting questions here are about how the slopes differ between schools (sections 6 to 8).

A multilevel model handles both. It has one equation for the students (level 1) and one for the schools (level 2). The same models are also called hierarchical linear models (HLM), mixed (effects) models and random-effects models. They are not the same as “hierarchical regression” in the sense of entering predictors in blocks and testing \(\Delta R^2\), which has its own tutorial: Hierarchical Regression.


Code
library(nlme)       # lme(): multilevel models (comes with R)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
1. The data
The nlme package has the students in MathAchieve and the schools in MathAchSchool. We join them and give the columns short names:


Code
students <- as.data.frame(MathAchieve)
hsb <- merge(students[, c("School", "Minority", "Sex", "SES", "MathAch")],
             MathAchSchool[, c("School", "Size", "Sector")], by = "School")
names(hsb) <- c("school", "minority", "sex", "ses", "math", "size", "sector")
hsb$school <- factor(hsb$school)

c(students = nrow(hsb), schools = nlevels(hsb$school))


students  schools 
    7185      160 


Code
table(sector = MathAchSchool$Sector)


sector
  Public Catholic 
      90       70 


Code
summary(as.numeric(table(hsb$school)))   # students per school


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  14.00   35.00   47.00   44.91   54.00   67.00 










Variable
Level
Meaning




math
student
Mathematics achievement test score (from -2.8 to 25)


ses
student
Socio-economic status: a standardised composite of parental education, occupation and income


school
school
School identifier: the grouping variable


sector
school
Public or Catholic




Splitting SES into a school part and a student part
A student’s SES says two things: how well off their family is, and (through their classmates) how well off their school is. We split it in two:


Code
hsb$ses_school <- ave(hsb$ses, hsb$school)       # the average SES of the student's school
hsb$ses_within <- hsb$ses - hsb$ses_school       # the student's SES compared with their schoolmates
head(hsb[, c("school", "sector", "ses", "ses_school", "ses_within", "math")])


  school sector    ses ses_school  ses_within   math
1   1224 Public -1.528  -0.434383 -1.09361702  5.876
2   1224 Public -0.588  -0.434383 -0.15361702 19.708
3   1224 Public -0.528  -0.434383 -0.09361702 20.349
4   1224 Public -0.668  -0.434383 -0.23361702  8.781
5   1224 Public -0.158  -0.434383  0.27638298 17.898
6   1224 Public  0.022  -0.434383  0.45638298  4.583



ses_school is the school mean SES: the same for every student of a school, so it is a school-level variable.
ses_within is the student’s SES centred within the school: positive for students better off than their schoolmates, negative for those worse off. Its mean in every school is 0.

This is called group-mean centring. Section 7 shows why it matters: the two parts have very different effects.

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
2. Look at the data
Eight schools, chosen at random, four of each sector. Each point is a student, and each line is an ordinary regression fitted to that school alone:


Code
set.seed(3)
pick <- c(sample(unique(as.character(hsb$school[hsb$sector == "Public"])), 4),
          sample(unique(as.character(hsb$school[hsb$sector == "Catholic"])), 4))
few <- subset(hsb, school %in% pick)
few$label <- with(few, paste0(sector, " school ", school, "\n(", ave(math, school, FUN = length), " students)"))
ggplot(few, aes(ses, math)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, aes(colour = sector), linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~label, ncol = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Public = "#0082c8", Catholic = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "Maths score against family SES in eight schools", x = "SES", y = "maths score") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









All 160 schools, one line per school, drawn over the range of ses_within of its students:


Code
per_school <- lmList(math ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)   # an ordinary regression in every school
ols <- data.frame(school = rownames(coef(per_school)), coef(per_school), check.names = FALSE)
names(ols)[2:3] <- c("intercept", "slope")
ols$sector <- MathAchSchool$Sector[match(ols$school, MathAchSchool$School)]
ols$n      <- as.numeric(table(hsb$school)[ols$school])
rng <- aggregate(ses_within ~ school, hsb, range)
ols$x0 <- rng$ses_within[match(ols$school, rng$school), 1]
ols$x1 <- rng$ses_within[match(ols$school, rng$school), 2]

ggplot(ols) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x0, xend = x1, y = intercept + slope * x0, yend = intercept + slope * x1, colour = sector),
               alpha = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~sector) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Public = "#0082c8", Catholic = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "One regression line per school", x = "SES compared with schoolmates (ses_within)",
       y = "maths score") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









Three things stand out:

The lines start at very different heights: some schools score much higher than others, whatever the SES of their students. The intercepts (the school averages) go from 4.2 to 19.7.
The slopes differ too: in some schools SES matters a lot, in others hardly at all (from -2 to 6.3). Some of this is real, and some is noise: a school of 14 students gives a very rough slope.
The Catholic lines look higher and flatter.

A multilevel model turns these impressions into estimates with honest uncertainty. We build it in steps, adding one idea at a time.

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
section: 3. Step 0: the null model, or how much do schools differ?
text:
3. Step 0: the null model, or how much do schools differ?
The simplest multilevel model has no predictors. Student \(i\) in school \(j\):
\[\text{Level 1 (students):}\qquad \text{math}_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + r_{ij}, \qquad r_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]
\[\text{Level 2 (schools):}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \qquad u_{0j} \sim N(0, \tau_{00})\]

\(\beta_{0j}\) is the average score of school \(j\).
\(\gamma_{00}\) (“gamma”) is the average over all schools: a fixed effect, one number for everyone.
\(u_{0j}\) is how far school \(j\) is from that average: a random effect, one per school. We do not estimate 160 separate numbers; we estimate their variance \(\tau_{00}\) (“tau”).
\(r_{ij}\) is how far student \(i\) is from their school’s average, with variance \(\sigma^2\).

Putting the two levels together gives one equation, which is what R fits: \(\text{math}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j} + r_{ij}\).


Code
m0 <- lme(math ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
summary(m0)


Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML
  Data: hsb 
       AIC      BIC   logLik
  47122.79 47143.43 -23558.4

Random effects:
 Formula: ~1 | school
        (Intercept) Residual
StdDev:    2.934966 6.256862

Fixed effects:  math ~ 1 
               Value Std.Error   DF  t-value p-value
(Intercept) 12.63697 0.2443936 7025 51.70747       0

Standardized Within-Group Residuals:
        Min          Q1         Med          Q3         Max 
-3.06312473 -0.75387398  0.02670132  0.76062171  2.74262579 

Number of Observations: 7185
Number of Groups: 160 



How to read the output

Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML: the estimation method. REML (restricted maximum likelihood) gives better variance estimates than ordinary maximum likelihood (ML). Section 9 explains when to switch to ML.
AIC, BIC, logLik: the fit of the model, used to compare models (lower AIC and BIC is better).
Random effects: the standard deviations of the random parts. (Intercept) is \(\sqrt{\tau_{00}}\), how much the school averages differ, and Residual is \(\sigma\), how much students differ within a school.
Fixed effects: the \(\gamma\)s, with standard errors, degrees of freedom, t and p, read like a regression table. Here there is only \(\gamma_{00}\) = 12.64, the average school score.
DF: lme() counts the degrees of freedom at the level of each predictor. Student-level effects get about as many as there are students, school-level effects about as many as there are schools (we will see 157 for them below).
Standardized Within-Group Residuals: a summary of the level-1 residuals; roughly symmetric around 0 is good.
Number of Observations and Number of Groups: 7185 students in 160 schools.



The intraclass correlation (ICC)
VarCorr() gives the variances:


Code
VarCorr(m0)


school = pdLogChol(1) 
            Variance  StdDev  
(Intercept)  8.614025 2.934966
Residual    39.148322 6.256862


Code
vc <- function(m) { v <- VarCorr(m); setNames(as.numeric(v[, "Variance"]), rownames(v)) }   # variances as numbers
tau00 <- vc(m0)["(Intercept)"]
sigma2 <- vc(m0)["Residual"]
icc <- unname(tau00 / (tau00 + sigma2))
icc


[1] 0.1803518


\[\text{ICC} = \frac{\tau_{00}}{\tau_{00} + \sigma^2} = \frac{8.61}{8.61 + 39.15} = 0.18\]
About 18% of the differences in maths scores lie between schools, and 82% between students of the same school. The ICC is also the correlation between the scores of two students of the same school. Any ICC above about 0.05 is a good reason for a multilevel model, and 0.18 is a lot.

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
4. What ignoring the schools does
Compare ordinary regression with a multilevel model that has the same two predictors, SES and sector:


Code
fit_ols <- lm(math ~ ses + sector, data = hsb)
fit_mlm <- lme(math ~ ses + sector, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
se_ols <- summary(fit_ols)$coefficients[, "Std. Error"]
se_mlm <- summary(fit_mlm)$tTable[, "Std.Error"]
round(data.frame(estimate_ols = coef(fit_ols), se_ols, estimate_mlm = fixef(fit_mlm), se_mlm,
                 se_ratio = se_mlm / se_ols), 3)


               estimate_ols se_ols estimate_mlm se_mlm se_ratio
(Intercept)          11.793  0.106       11.719  0.228    2.149
ses                   2.949  0.098        2.375  0.105    1.078
sectorCatholic        1.935  0.152        2.101  0.341    2.237


The Catholic coefficient has a standard error 2.2 times larger in the multilevel model. Ordinary regression acts as if it had 7,185 independent pieces of information about Catholic schools. In fact there are only 160 schools, and the students of each school share most of what makes their school different.
The design effect says how much the clustering inflates the variance of an estimate. With \(\bar m\) students per school:
\[\text{design effect} = 1 + (\bar m - 1) \times \text{ICC} = 1 + (44.9 - 1) \times 0.18 = 8.9\]
so standard errors of school-level effects can be up to \(\sqrt{8.9} = 3\) times too small. (The ratio above is smaller because SES already explains part of the differences between schools.) Too-small standard errors mean confidence intervals that are too narrow and p values that are too small: findings that look stronger than they are.

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
5. Step 1: a student-level predictor
Now add the student’s SES, centred within the school:
\[\text{Level 1:}\qquad \text{math}_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + r_{ij}\]
\[\text{Level 2:}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \qquad \beta_{1} = \gamma_{10}\]
The slope \(\beta_1\) is the same in every school for now (it has no \(u\)).


Code
m1 <- lme(math ~ ses_within, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
summary(m1)$tTable


                Value Std.Error   DF  t-value      p-value
(Intercept) 12.636139 0.2444873 7024 51.68422 0.000000e+00
ses_within   2.191172 0.1086546 7024 20.16640 5.756752e-88


Code
VarCorr(m1)


school = pdLogChol(1) 
            Variance  StdDev  
(Intercept)  8.672288 2.944875
Residual    37.010413 6.083618


Within a school, a student one SD higher in SES than their schoolmates scores about 2.19 points higher.
How much did SES explain? Compare the variances with the null model. The proportion by which a variance shrinks is the multilevel version of \(R^2\), one for each level:


Code
c(sigma2_null = unname(sigma2), sigma2_step1 = unname(vc(m1)["Residual"]),
  level1_R2 = unname(1 - vc(m1)["Residual"] / sigma2))


 sigma2_null sigma2_step1    level1_R2 
 39.14832200  37.01041300   0.05461049 


SES explains about 5.5% of the differences between students of the same school. The school variance \(\tau_{00}\) did not go down (8.67, against 8.61): it cannot, because ses_within has the same mean, 0, in every school. To explain why schools differ we need school-level predictors (section 7).

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
section: 6. Step 2: random slopes, or does family background matter equally in every school?
text:
6. Step 2: random slopes, or does family background matter equally in every school?
Let the slope differ between schools:
\[\text{Level 1:}\qquad \text{math}_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + r_{ij}\]
\[\text{Level 2:}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \qquad \beta_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + u_{1j}\]
Now each school has its own slope \(\beta_{1j}\), spread around the average slope \(\gamma_{10}\) with variance \(\tau_{11}\). The intercepts and slopes may be correlated, with covariance \(\tau_{01}\). In R, random = ~ ses_within | school means “an intercept and a ses_within slope for every school”:


Code
m2 <- lme(math ~ ses_within, random = ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)
summary(m2)$tTable


                Value Std.Error   DF  t-value      p-value
(Intercept) 12.636193 0.2445038 7024 51.68097 0.000000e+00
ses_within   2.193196 0.1282586 7024 17.09980 2.936628e-64


Code
VarCorr(m2)


school = pdLogChol(ses_within) 
            Variance   StdDev    Corr  
(Intercept)  8.6809690 2.9463484 (Intr)
ses_within   0.6939876 0.8330592 0.019 
Residual    36.7002004 6.0580690       


Code
tau11 <- unname(vc(m2)["ses_within"])



The average slope is still about 2.19.
The slopes vary with a standard deviation of \(\sqrt{\tau_{11}}\) = 0.83. If they are normally distributed, about 95% of schools have a slope between \(2.19 \pm 1.96 \times 0.83\), that is from 0.56 to 3.83. In practically every school richer students do better, but in some schools the gap is several times larger than in others.
Corr is the correlation of the intercepts and slopes, near 0 here: high-scoring schools do not have steeper or flatter slopes.


Is the slope variance real? A likelihood-ratio test
Compare the models with and without the random slope:


Code
lrt <- anova(m1, m2)
lrt


   Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test  L.Ratio p-value
m1     1  4 46732.00 46759.51 -23362.00                        
m2     2  6 46726.23 46767.51 -23357.12 1 vs 2 9.761657  0.0076


The random slope adds two parameters (the variance \(\tau_{11}\) and the covariance \(\tau_{01}\)), and the likelihood-ratio test (L.Ratio) is 9.76, p = 0.0076. Both models have the same fixed effects, so comparing their REML fits is fine.
The p value is conservative (too large). The test asks whether \(\tau_{11} = 0\), and a variance cannot be negative, so 0 is at the edge of its possible values. The correct reference distribution is a 50:50 mixture of \(\chi^2\) with 1 and 2 degrees of freedom (Self & Liang, 1987; Stram & Lee, 1994):


Code
LR <- lrt$L.Ratio[2]
c(p_naive = pchisq(LR, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE),
  p_mixture = 0.5 * pchisq(LR, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) + 0.5 * pchisq(LR, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE))


    p_naive   p_mixture 
0.007590724 0.004686308 


Either way, the SES gap does differ between schools.


The same sequence with one call: report_hlr()
The rwf package fits this sequence of models in one call: no random effect at all (an ordinary regression fitted with gls()), a random intercept, the predictor, and a random slope, compared step by step with likelihood-ratio tests. It uses ML (see section 9), so the numbers differ slightly from the REML fits above:


Code
steps <- report_hlr(df = hsb, corlist = which(names(hsb) == "math"), factorlist = which(names(hsb) == "school"),
                    predictor = "ses_within", random_effect = "school")
steps[, c("model", "fixed", "random", "df", "AIC", "BIC", "logLik", "Test", "L.Ratio", "p.value")]


                       model             fixed               random df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test    L.Ratio       p.value
1                       base          math ~ 1                 <NA>  2 48103.73 48117.49 -24049.87                NA            NA
2           random_intercept          math ~ 1          ~1 | school  3 47121.81 47142.45 -23557.91 1 vs 2 983.921822 5.611909e-216
3 random_intercept_predictor math ~ ses_within          ~1 | school  4 46728.41 46755.93 -23360.21 2 vs 3 395.398363  5.529267e-88
4     random_intercept_slope math ~ ses_within ~ses_within | school  6 46722.98 46764.26 -23355.49 3 vs 4   9.433005  8.946412e-03


Read it row by row. The first test (1 vs 2) asks whether schools differ at all: an enormous likelihood ratio, the ICC of section 3 in test form. The second (2 vs 3) tests SES, the third (3 vs 4) the random slope.


What the model believes about each school: shrinkage
The model gives an estimate of the intercept and slope of every school (coef(m2)). They are not the same as the separate regressions of section 2:


Code
eb <- coef(m2)                                   # the multilevel estimate for each school
ols$intercept_mlm <- eb[ols$school, "(Intercept)"]
ols$slope_mlm     <- eb[ols$school, "ses_within"]
g <- fixef(m2)
s1 <- ggplot(ols, aes(intercept, intercept_mlm, size = n)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = g[1], colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0082c8") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Intercepts (school averages)", x = "separate regression", y = "multilevel model", size = "students")
s2 <- ggplot(ols, aes(slope, slope_mlm, size = n)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = g[2], colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0082c8") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "SES slopes", x = "separate regression", y = "multilevel model", size = "students")
s1 + s2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")   # one legend for both panels









Code
round(rbind(separate_regressions = range(ols$slope), multilevel_model = range(ols$slope_mlm)), 2)


                      [,1] [,2]
separate_regressions -2.02 6.27
multilevel_model      0.78 3.41


The multilevel estimates are pulled from the dashed diagonal (each school on its own) towards the red line (the average of all schools). This is called shrinkage, and the estimates are called empirical Bayes estimates. For a school average in the random-intercept model the formula is:
\[\hat\beta_{0j} = \lambda_j\,\bar y_j + (1 - \lambda_j)\,\hat\gamma_{00}, \qquad \lambda_j = \frac{\tau_{00}}{\tau_{00} + \sigma^2 / n_j}\]
\(\lambda_j\) is the reliability of school \(j\)’s own mean: close to 1 when the school has many students (its own mean is trustworthy), smaller when it has few. In the null model:


Code
n_j <- as.numeric(table(hsb$school))
lambda <- tau00 / (tau00 + sigma2 / n_j)
round(c(smallest_school = min(lambda), median = median(lambda), largest_school = max(lambda)), 2)


smallest_school          median  largest_school 
           0.75            0.91            0.94 


The slopes shrink much more than the intercepts. A slope estimated from 14 to 67 students is very noisy, and the slopes truly differ only a little (\(\sqrt{\tau_{11}}\) = 0.83), so most of the spread of the separate slopes (from -2 to 6.3) is noise. The model keeps the part it believes is real (from 0.8 to 3.4). The negative slopes of a few small schools were flukes.

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
section: 7. Step 3: school-level predictors, within and between
text:
7. Step 3: school-level predictors, within and between
Why do some schools score higher? Add two school-level predictors to the intercept equation: the school’s mean SES and its sector (Catholic = 1, public = 0):
\[\text{Level 2:}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{ses\_school}_j + \gamma_{02}\,\text{Catholic}_j + u_{0j}, \qquad \beta_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + u_{1j}\]


Code
m3 <- lme(math ~ ses_within + ses_school + sector, random = ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)
summary(m3)$tTable


                   Value Std.Error   DF   t-value      p-value
(Intercept)    12.063419 0.1991480 7024 60.575153 0.000000e+00
ses_within      2.194980 0.1284185 7024 17.092388 3.317645e-64
ses_school      5.246300 0.3683306  157 14.243455 4.423748e-30
sectorCatholic  1.372171 0.3055220  157  4.491234 1.365339e-05


Code
VarCorr(m3)


school = pdLogChol(ses_within) 
            Variance   StdDev   Corr  
(Intercept)  2.3851744 1.544401 (Intr)
ses_within   0.7006628 0.837056 0.18  
Residual    36.7097503 6.058857       



Catholic schools score 1.37 points higher than public schools with the same mean SES.
Note the DF: 157 for the school-level predictors, because there are 160 schools; 7024 for the student-level one.
The school variance fell from 8.68 to 2.39: school SES and sector explain 73% of the differences between school averages.


Within and between: two different SES effects
The two SES coefficients are very different:

Within a school, one SD more family SES goes with 2.19 points more.
Between schools, a school whose students are on average one SD better off scores 5.25 points higher.

The difference is the contextual effect: the extra score that comes from being in a better-off school, for two students with the same family SES. To get it directly, with its own standard error, use the uncentred SES together with the school mean (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002). There the school-mean coefficient is the contextual effect:


Code
m_ctx <- lme(math ~ ses + ses_school, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
summary(m_ctx)$tTable


                Value Std.Error   DF  t-value      p-value
(Intercept) 12.683308 0.1493802 7024 84.90621 0.000000e+00
ses          2.191172 0.1086673 7024 20.16404 6.021818e-88
ses_school   3.675002 0.3776705  158  9.73071 7.953398e-18


Two students from equally well-off families differ by about 3.7 points if one attends a school whose mean SES is one unit higher.
What if we had not split SES? A model with the raw SES only gives a single slope:


Code
m_raw <- lme(math ~ ses, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
round(c(raw_ses_slope = unname(fixef(m_raw)["ses"]), within = unname(fixef(m3)["ses_within"]),
        between = unname(fixef(m3)["ses_school"])), 2)


raw_ses_slope        within       between 
         2.39          2.19          5.25 


The raw slope (2.39) is a blend of the within and the between effects, and answers neither question. Decide which question you are asking, and centre accordingly (Enders & Tofighi, 2007):

Group-mean centring (ses_within, plus ses_school at level 2) separates the within and the between effects. Use it when the student-level effect is the question, and for random slopes.
Grand-mean centring (SES minus the overall mean) keeps the blend but makes the intercept the score of an average student. Use it when the student-level predictor is only a control.

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
section: 8. Step 4: cross-level interactions, or why do slopes differ?
text:
8. Step 4: cross-level interactions, or why do slopes differ?
Section 6 showed that the SES gap differs between schools. Can school characteristics explain why? Put the school predictors into the slope equation too:
\[\beta_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{ses\_school}_j + \gamma_{12}\,\text{Catholic}_j + u_{1j}\]
Substituting into level 1 gives products of a student-level and a school-level variable: cross-level interactions.
\[\text{math}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{ses\_school}_j + \gamma_{02}\,\text{Catholic}_j + \gamma_{10}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{ses\_school}_j \times \text{ses\_within}_{ij} + \gamma_{12}\,\text{Catholic}_j \times \text{ses\_within}_{ij} + u_{0j} + u_{1j}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + r_{ij}\]
In R, ses_within * (ses_school + sector) writes all of these terms:


Code
m4 <- lme(math ~ ses_within * (ses_school + sector), random = ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)
summary(m4)$tTable


                              Value Std.Error   DF   t-value      p-value
(Intercept)               12.127931 0.1992951 7022 60.854147 0.000000e+00
ses_within                 2.945043 0.1555906 7022 18.928149 5.697836e-78
ses_school                 5.332878 0.3691743  157 14.445420 1.255094e-30
sectorCatholic             1.226578 0.3062783  157  4.004782 9.554485e-05
ses_within:ses_school      1.039249 0.2988794 7022  3.477152 5.098400e-04
ses_within:sectorCatholic -1.642680 0.2397649 7022 -6.851211 7.943710e-12


Code
VarCorr(m4)


school = pdLogChol(ses_within) 
            Variance   StdDev    Corr  
(Intercept)  2.3797629 1.5426480 (Intr)
ses_within   0.1010237 0.3178422 0.391 
Residual    36.7211868 6.0598009       


Code
b4 <- fixef(m4)


Read the interactions as changes in the SES slope:

In a public school of average SES, the SES slope is 2.95.
In a Catholic school of average SES, it is 2.95 \(-\) 1.64 = 1.30: the gap between richer and poorer students is less than half as large.
In better-off schools the slope is steeper: 1.04 more per unit of school mean SES.

The slope variance fell from 0.70 to 0.10: sector and school SES explain 86% of the differences in SES slopes. Is any slope variance left?


Code
m4_no_slope <- update(m4, random = ~ 1 | school)
anova(m4_no_slope, m4)


            Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test  L.Ratio p-value
m4_no_slope     1  8 46520.79 46575.82 -23252.39                        
m4              2 10 46523.66 46592.45 -23251.83 1 vs 2 1.124097    0.57


No (p = 0.57, and still clearly above .05 after halving it for the boundary). Once we know a school’s sector and mean SES, its SES slope is predictable; the remaining differences between schools are in their average scores. A simpler final model with a random intercept only would be defensible here; we keep the random slope to show the full model.
The model’s predictions show the pattern:


Code
grid <- expand.grid(ses_within = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 50), sector = c("Public", "Catholic"),
                    ses_school = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5))
grid$sector <- factor(grid$sector, levels = levels(hsb$sector))
grid$math <- predict(m4, newdata = grid, level = 0)        # level = 0: the fixed effects, for a typical school
grid$school_ses <- factor(grid$ses_school, labels = c("poorer schools (mean SES -0.5)", "average schools (0)",
                                                      "richer schools (+0.5)"))
ggplot(grid, aes(ses_within, math, colour = sector)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~school_ses) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Public = "#0082c8", Catholic = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "Predicted maths score: the SES gap is smaller in Catholic schools",
       x = "SES compared with schoolmates", y = "predicted maths score", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The Catholic advantage is largest for the students who are worse off than their schoolmates. For students well above their schoolmates the two sectors predict about the same score, and the lines cross. Richer schools (right) score higher in both sectors and have steeper lines.
A word of caution: students are not randomly assigned to Catholic schools. Families who choose them may differ in ways that SES does not capture, so these are associations, not proof that Catholic schools cause a smaller gap (Coleman et al., 1982, started a long debate about exactly this).

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
9. Comparing all the models
REML or ML? REML estimates the variances better, so report REML fits. But REML likelihoods can only be compared between models with the same fixed effects (as in section 6). To test fixed effects with a likelihood-ratio test, refit with method = "ML":


Code
anova(update(m2, method = "ML"), update(m3, method = "ML"), update(m4, method = "ML"))


                          Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test   L.Ratio p-value
update(m2, method = "ML")     1  6 46722.98 46764.26 -23355.49                         
update(m3, method = "ML")     2  8 46554.14 46609.18 -23269.07 1 vs 2 172.83591  <.0001
update(m4, method = "ML")     3 10 46516.43 46585.23 -23248.21 2 vs 3  41.71416  <.0001


Both steps improve the model a lot. All the models side by side:


Code
models <- list("0: null" = m0, "1: + SES within" = m1, "2: + random slope" = m2,
               "3: + school SES, sector" = m3, "4: + cross-level interactions" = m4)
get_v <- function(m, name) { v <- vc(m); if (name %in% names(v)) unname(v[name]) else NA }
round(t(sapply(models, function(m) {
  ml <- update(m, method = "ML")
  c(tau00 = get_v(m, "(Intercept)"), tau11 = get_v(m, "ses_within"), sigma2 = get_v(m, "Residual"),
    parameters = attr(logLik(ml), "df"), AIC_ML = AIC(ml), BIC_ML = BIC(ml))
})), 2)

1: + SES within                8.67    NA  37.01          4 46728.41 46755.93

3: + school SES, sector        2.39  0.70  36.71          8 46554.14 46609.18

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
10. Checking the assumptions
A multilevel model assumes, at each level, normally distributed random parts with constant variance: the student residuals \(r_{ij}\) and the school effects \(u_{0j}\) and \(u_{1j}\).


Code
d <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(m4), residual = resid(m4, type = "normalized"))
re <- ranef(m4)
qq <- function(x, title) ggplot(data.frame(x = x), aes(sample = x)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#0082c8") + stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = title, x = "normal quantiles", y = "sample quantiles")
d1 <- ggplot(d, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#E74C3C") +
  labs(title = "Student residuals against fitted", x = "fitted maths score", y = "standardised residual")
(d1 + qq(d$residual, "Student residuals")) / (qq(re[, "(Intercept)"], "School intercepts (u0)") +
                                              qq(re[, "ses_within"], "School slopes (u1)"))










Student residuals against fitted: a band around 0 with no curve in it. Its sharp upper edge on the right is the ceiling of the test: the top score is 25, so a student predicted to score 20 cannot be more than 5 points above the prediction. The lower edge on the left is the floor, for the same reason.
Student residuals: close to the line in the middle; the tails are shorter than those of a normal distribution, again because of the floor and the ceiling. With 7,185 students, this hardly affects the estimates.
School intercepts and slopes: close to the line. With 160 schools that is what matters for the level-2 estimates. The slopes are strongly shrunken (section 6), so their spread is small.

11. The same models in lme4
The lme4 package is the other common choice. Its lmer() writes the random part inside the formula, in brackets:

round(cbind(nlme = fixef(m4), lme4 = lme4::fixef(m4_lmer)), 3)

ses_school                 5.333  5.333

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
section: 12. Reporting the results in APA style
text:
12. Reporting the results in APA style
A report (APA 7th edition) should give the structure of the data, the ICC, how the model was built, the fixed effects with their uncertainty, the variance components, and the tests of the random effects. We collect the numbers from the R objects:


Code
tt  <- summary(m4)$tTable
ci  <- intervals(m4, which = "fixed")$fixed
v4  <- vc(m4)
lr_slope <- anova(m1, m2)
ml_test  <- anova(update(m3, method = "ML"), update(m4, method = "ML"))

f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))


Method (data analysis):

Mathematics achievement scores of 7,185 students nested in 160 high schools (70 Catholic, 90 public; 14 to 67 students per school) were analysed with two-level linear models (students within schools), estimated by restricted maximum likelihood in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the nlme package. Student socio-economic status (SES) was centred on the school mean, and the school mean SES was entered as a school-level predictor. Models were built in steps: a null model, student SES, a random SES slope, school-level predictors (mean SES and sector), and cross-level interactions. Fixed effects were compared with likelihood-ratio tests of maximum-likelihood fits.

Results:

In the null model, 18% of the variance in mathematics achievement lay between schools (ICC = .18). Students with higher SES than their schoolmates scored higher, and this within-school SES slope varied between schools, χ²(2) = 9.76, p = .008. In the final model (Table 1), students in Catholic schools scored higher than students in public schools with the same mean SES, b = 1.23, 95% CI [0.62, 1.83], and school mean SES was strongly related to achievement, b = 5.33, 95% CI [4.60, 6.06]. The within-school SES slope was 2.95 in public schools of average SES, smaller in Catholic schools, b = -1.64, 95% CI [-2.11, -1.17], and larger in schools with higher mean SES, b = 1.04, 95% CI [0.45, 1.63]. Adding the cross-level interactions improved the model, χ²(2) = 41.71, p < .001, and reduced the slope variance by 86%.

Points to remember:

Report the ICC of the null model, and the number of groups and of observations per group.
Say how the predictors were centred: it changes what the coefficients mean.
Report the variance components, not only the fixed effects, and how the random slopes were tested (and that the test is conservative, or corrected for the boundary).
Say whether the likelihood-ratio tests of fixed effects used ML fits.
Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("nlme") in R give the exact references.

title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
text:
13. Summary







When
Observations come in groups (students in schools, employees in teams, patients in hospitals, repeated measurements in people)


Why not OLS
Observations in a group are alike (ICC > 0), so standard errors are too small, especially for group-level predictors


Step 0: null model
lme(y ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | g); ICC = \(\tau_{00} / (\tau_{00} + \sigma^2)\)


Level-1 predictors
Centre within the group to get the within effect; add the group mean for the between effect


Random slopes
random = ~ x | g; test with a likelihood-ratio test, which is conservative at the boundary


Level-2 predictors
Explain the differences between group averages (less \(\tau_{00}\))


Cross-level interactions
x * w, with x at level 1 and w at level 2: explain why slopes differ (less \(\tau_{11}\))


Estimation
REML to report; ML to compare models with different fixed effects


Group estimates
Shrunk towards the average, more so for small groups and noisy slopes


R
nlme::lme(), or lme4::lmer() with lmerTest for p values; rwf::report_hlr() for the step-by-step sequence
